+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A small display screen on the wall cycles through various system diagnostics in green text. PRESSURE NOMINAL. O2 21.3%. INERTIAL DAMPERS ONLINE. The letters flicker, refresh, flicker again, as if the ship itself were breathing. Arthur Neegan watched them from the jump seat bolted to the bulkhead of the transfer vessel *Ares Courier*. The cabin smelled of recycled air and hot plastic. Through the narrow viewport, Mars was already a thin rust-colored crescent, and beyond it nothing but black. He had been given a uniform that was too big, a data-slate he was not allowed to touch, and two men who never left his sight. They wore the grey-blue of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. The insignia on their collars — a stylized star with three concentric rings — was embroidered in dull silver. Diplomatic in name only, the local miners said. The Corps brought messages. Sometimes it brought guns. “First time off-planet?” one of them asked without looking up from his console. Arthur forced a smile. “First time off my claim.” The man grunted. “You’re lucky. Most engineers don’t get invited to tea.” The ship shuddered as the transfer tug detached. Arthur’s stomach lurched. He thought of his wife Mara in the hab-dome, of the survey rig he’d left half-buried in permafrost, of the vein his ground-penetrating lidar had found under Plot 7-B. A vein of Azra wide enough to make a man rich and a planet a target. He had not wanted any of it. The hatch hissed. A woman stepped in, and the two guards snapped to attention. She was not in uniform. Her suit was civilian, cut for low gravity, the color of old paper. Her hair was pulled back severely. A small lapel pin caught the cabin light — the same Antares star, but with a single red dot at its center. “Mr. Neegan,” she said. Her voice was calm, precise, with the faint clipped accent of the inner worlds. “I am Lia Chen. I represent the interests of the Antares Concord. Please, sit.” Arthur sat. The diagnostics screen ticked over to NAV LOCK ACQUIRED. “Your claim is impressive,” Chen said, taking the seat opposite him. She did not offer her hand. “A deposit of that purity, that depth, on a first-generation settler’s lease. Statistically improbable. Geologically fascinating.” “I’m a mining engineer,” Arthur said. “I know where to look.” “Do you know what you’ve found?” “I know it’s Azra. I know it decays everything around it. I know three corporations already offered me enough money to buy the whole of Acidalia Planitia.” Chen nodded once. “Hegemony Mining, Vesta Dynamics, and the Martian Development Authority. All very polite. All very interested in weapons.” The ship gave a soft chime. The green text changed to TRANSIT STABLE. “Azra does not merely accelerate radioactive decay,” Chen said. “It accelerates it *selectively*. Under controlled conditions, it can be made to skip steps. A gram properly tuned can make a reactor burn for a century or a day. It can make a warhead burn through a shield. The physics are still being argued in the academies on Luna and in the Council chambers on Earth.” She leaned forward. “The problem, Mr. Neegan, is that nobody understands it yet. The corporations want to mine it blindly, refine it, sell it. The Hegemony wants to weaponize it. The Martian Free Council wants to nationalize it. All of them will kill to get it, and all of them will use it badly.” Arthur swallowed. “And you?” “We want to study it,” Chen said. “Properly. With the men who found it.” “You want me.” “I want your expertise, your claim, and your discretion. In return, the Concord will grant you full Martian citizenship, a research stipend that will make your family comfortable for three generations, and a guarantee that Plot 7-B will never be strip-mined.” “Why me?” “Because you are not a corporate man. You are a settler. You built your dome with your own hands. People like you are why Mars was colonized in the first place — not for gold rushes, but for a future.” She smiled thinly. “The big picture, Mr. Neegan, is that humanity is spreading too fast for one government to hold. Earth is tired. Antares is rising. Mars is caught in the middle. Azra is the fulcrum. If it falls into the wrong hands, the next war will not be fought over water or land. It will be fought over time itself.” Arthur looked at the green diagnostics. PRESSURE NOMINAL. “What’s the small picture?” he asked. Chen’s expression softened, almost imperceptibly. “The small picture is that your wife is still on Mars, and the men who came to your door this morning are not the last who will come. The corporations have already filed injunctions on your lease. The Development Authority has a warrant for ‘unauthorized extraction.’ You have about forty-eight hours before someone tries to take it by force.” She slid a data-slate across the table. On it was a contract, already signed on one side. “Sign, and we evacuate Mara and your children to a Concord habitat in orbit. You come with us to Antares Station. You work with our physicists. You tell us what you saw in the rock, and we make sure no one else ever has to bleed for it.” Arthur stared at the screen. The green text cycled to LIFE SUPPORT NOMINAL. “Or I refuse,” he said quietly. “Then you will be a very rich, very dead man,” Chen said, not unkindly. “And Mars will have another ghost town.” Outside the viewport, the stars were coming out. Arthur thought of the vein beneath his feet, humming with invisible decay, waiting to be touched. He thought of Mara’s hands in the soil, of the first seedlings he’d coaxed to grow under red light. He picked up the slate. “One condition,” he said. “I don’t want to make weapons.” Chen stood. “Mr. Neegan,” she said, “that is the only thing we want either.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and prompt requirements. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere with technical details like "PRESSURE NOMINAL. O2 21.3%. INERTIAL DAMPERS ONLINE" and maintains the retrofuturistic feel throughout. The dialogue-heavy structure works well, with Chen serving as an effective exposition vehicle while maintaining character agency. The world-building effectively balances big-picture elements (interplanetary politics, the nature of Azra, humanity's expansion) with intimate details (Arthur's personal stakes, his family, his individual claim). The political intrigue is well-established through corporate interests, diplomatic maneuvering, and the larger implications of Azra technology. Character motivations feel authentic - Arthur as the reluctant everyman caught in forces beyond his control, and Chen as the pragmatic representative of larger interests. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and building the world. The prose maintains an appropriate tone throughout, neither too sparse nor overwrought. Technical details are woven naturally into the narrative. The pacing builds tension effectively toward Arthur's decision. However, the piece has some limitations. While competent, it doesn't break significant new ground in terms of creativity or surprise. The scenario of the small person caught between large forces is familiar, though well-executed. Some dialogue moments, particularly Chen's exposition about Azra's properties, lean slightly toward tell-don't-show, though this is somewhat mitigated by the conversational context. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - Arthur makes a pragmatic choice based on the information presented, and the final exchange about not making weapons provides appropriate moral grounding without being saccharine. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smells like vinegar and warm metal. Red light makes everything look like a secret. I’m 25 and I know how to take up space. In critique I’m the one who leans forward, elbows on the table, and says “no, you’re not done yet.” I wear black leather pants to class and my hair is dyed the color of a bruise. Boys my age call me intimidating. I like it. I like being the one who decides. Elliot is 19. He sits three rows down in experimental photo and never raises his hand. He wears thrift-store nu-goth like he found it in a dream — oversized black cardigan with moth holes, silver rings on every finger, hair dyed a washed-out blue that’s growing out at the roots. He’s soft in a way that makes my chest do something annoying. Quiet intellect. He watches the projector like he’s listening to it. Professor paired us for the final. “Late nights in the darkroom,” she said. “You’ll learn to trust each other.” I rolled my eyes at the time. Now it’s 11:47 p.m. and it’s just us. The enlarger hums. The timer ticks. Elliot is waiting for his first print to come up in the developer tray, and he’s humming. It’s low, tuneless, something he must have heard on the bus. The red light turns his cheeks pink and makes his eyelashes look ridiculous. I want to tell him to stop humming. I want to tell him it’s perfect. “Your contact sheet is good,” I say, because I’m Dani and I give notes. “You’re overexposing the shadows on purpose. It’s a choice.” He doesn’t look up. “It’s a mistake,” he says. “I keep thinking I’m doing it on purpose to make it look like I know what I’m doing.” I should take charge. That’s my default. I should say, *No, you do know. You’re good.* Instead I watch the image bloom in the tray. A hallway in his building at 3 a.m., empty, fluorescent buzz. “It looks lonely,” I say. “It’s supposed to be,” he says. “I took it after my roommate came home with someone.” The red light makes it hard to read faces. It makes it easier to say things. He dips the print in the stop bath, hands shaking a little. “Can I ask you something?” I nod, because I’m already leaning in too far. “I’ve been… I don’t know. Questioning.” He says it like he’s testing the word for weight. “My gender. Expression. Stuff. I’ve been reading about it for months. I don’t want to be… I don’t know what I want to be. I just know the way I dress makes people look at me weird and I like it and I hate it.” My first instinct is to fix it. To tell him he’s fine, he’s perfect, he’s exactly the kind of beautiful that art school pretends to want. That’s what I do with people I like — I take the wheel. But Elliot isn’t a project. He’s humming again, softer. “I’m he/him,” he adds quickly, like an apology. “Mostly. For now. I just… I don’t want you to think I’m trying to be something I’m not. I’m not trying to be a girl. I’m just trying to be less… loud? Or more? I don’t know.” I’ve always been attracted to definition. Broad shoulders, a jawline, someone who knows what he wants and wants me. Elliot is definition with the edges smudged. He’s a boy who looks like a ghost of a boy who looks like a girl who looks like no one. And I’m fascinated. I’m also terrified because if I say the wrong thing I’ll be the 25-year-old art bitch who made the 19-year-old kid feel small. So I do the thing I never do. I wait. The print is coming up. It’s the hallway, but now you can see the scuff marks on the floor, the way the light bleeds. “You’re allowed to not know,” I say. My voice sounds too big in the small room. I try again, smaller. “I think you’re allowed to not know for a long time.” He exhales. “You’re not mad?” “I’m not mad,” I say. “I’m… I’m trying not to make this about me.” It is about me. That’s the problem. I’m watching him find language for himself and I want to be there when he finds it. I want to be the person he tells first. That’s a take-charge impulse dressed up as support. Elliot pulls the print out, holds it up to the red light. “Do you think it’s good?” “It’s honest,” I say. “That’s better.” He smiles, just a little. The red light makes his teeth look white. He looks at me, really looks, and I realize I’ve been staring at his hands. The rings. The way he’s always fidgeting with them. “Can I ask you something?” he says. “Always,” I say, and then immediately regret how eager I sound. “Why do you like me?” The timer dings. The chemical smell spikes. I could lie. I could say it’s his work. I could say it’s his style. I could say it’s the way he hums while he waits for images to appear, like he’s coaxing them into being. Instead I say, “I don’t know yet. I think I’m used to people who are already decided. You’re… you’re in process. It’s exciting.” He blinks. “That’s a weird compliment.” “It’s the only one I have right now.” We stand there in the red dark, two people who are supposed to be making art about seeing. The print is drying on the line. Elliot’s humming again, and this time I can hear the tune — it’s something old, maybe his mom used to sing. I want to take charge and tell him I’ll protect him. I want to give him agency and shut up. I settle for handing him the tongs. “You do the next one,” I say. “I’ll watch.” He takes them. His fingers brush mine. The red light makes everything look like a confession booth, and for the first time in my life I’m not the one leading the prayer. I’m just sitting in the dark with someone, waiting for an image to come up, and hoping I don’t ruin it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's complex requirements, successfully capturing Dani's perspective as she navigates an intimate moment with Elliot in the darkroom setting. The author effectively establishes Dani's assertive personality through concrete details like her leather pants, bruise-colored hair, and take-charge attitude in critiques, then skillfully shows how this confidence wavers when confronted with Elliot's vulnerability. The characterization is particularly nuanced. Dani's internal conflict between her desire to "fix" and protect versus giving Elliot agency feels authentic and psychologically complex. Her admission "I'm trying not to make this about me" followed immediately by "It is about me. That's the problem" shows sophisticated self-awareness. Elliot's tentative exploration of gender identity is handled with sensitivity, avoiding both oversimplification and melodrama. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized, with the red light serving as both atmospheric detail and metaphor for the confessional nature of their conversation. The photography elements are woven naturally into the narrative rather than feeling forced or researched. The prose style effectively mirrors Dani's personality - direct, observational, with moments of unexpected vulnerability. Sentences like "He's definition with the edges smudged" and "You're in process. It's exciting" capture her artistic sensibility while revealing character growth. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The attraction dynamic could be explored more deeply - while the piece establishes Dani's fascination with Elliot's "unconventional masculinity," the specific nature of her evolving attraction remains somewhat abstract. The ending, while appropriately tentative, might benefit from slightly more emotional resonance. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, particularly Elliot's hesitant self-revelation and Dani's struggle to respond appropriately. The piece avoids common pitfalls of overwrought emotion or unearned transformation, instead presenting a realistic snapshot of two people in a moment of genuine connection and uncertainty. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Trevi Fountain was already sweating at nine in the morning. Ben had his guidebook open to *Baroque Fountains of Rome* and was trying to pronounce *Acqua Vergine* correctly when the Vespa screamed around the corner. Alessandra braked hard enough that the back wheel skidded on the tourists’ pigeons. “Madonna!” she shouted, not at him, at the world. “You’re going to walk into the fountain, professor?” “I — I’m so sorry — I didn’t see you —” Ben fumbled, clutching the guidebook to his chest like a shield. “Are you alright? Your bike —” She was already off the saddle, helmet tucked under one arm, hair a dark flag in the Roman heat. “I’m Alessandra. You’re the one who reads while crossing the street. Very British.” “I’m Ben. Ben Whitaker. I’m on sabbatical. From Oxford. I’m —” “On sabbatical from common sense,” she said, grinning. “You owe me a coffee. For the adrenaline.” He laughed, too quickly. “I would be delighted.” She swung a leg back over the Vespa. “Get on.” “Excuse me?” “Back. Now. You’re late for your tour.” ### The Vespa smelled of gasoline and citrus. Ben held on to the strap behind her seat while Rome blurred past — laundry lines, scooters, a priest on a bicycle. “Where are we going?” he shouted over the engine. “Somewhere the guidebook doesn’t know!” She cut through Via del Corso, then down a side street so narrow Ben’s elbow brushed a shutter. She stopped abruptly in front of a tiny bar with no sign. Inside, the barista knew her. “Caffè, per favore,” she said, then to Ben, rapid-fire: “Un cappuccino, and don’t look at me like that, you’re not in a library.” He ordered in halting Italian. The barista corrected him gently. Alessandra watched, amused. When the cups came, she lifted a sugar packet from the dispenser, tucked it into her palm, and palmed it into her jacket pocket while reaching for his cup. A small, practiced motion. Ben noticed the empty dispenser and then her hand, and looked away, embarrassed for noticing. “Grazie,” she said, too brightly. ### Campo de’ Fiori at noon was a riot of tomatoes and shouting. Alessandra ducked under a stall of lemons, grabbed a ripe cherry from a pile, popped it, and handed him the stem. “Try. It’s better than your tea.” Ben chewed, surprised. “It’s — it’s incredible.” She was already moving, dragging him past a tourist trap selling miniature Colosseums. A child’s bracelet of cheap blue beads caught her eye. She brushed past the vendor, her fingers lingering a half-second too long. The beads were gone by the time Ben turned back. “You’re very fast,” he said. “You’re very slow,” she said, and kissed his cheek, quick and startling. “Don’t be late.” ### They ate supplì standing up in a piazza off Trastevere. Ben was trying to explain his research on 17th-century epistolary culture when a man in a faded leather jacket stopped at their table. “Alessandra. Still stealing hearts?” She didn’t look up. “Marco. Still selling dreams?” He turned to Ben. “You’re the new one. Listen to me, *inglese*. She’s a beautiful disaster. She’ll take your wallet and your dignity and thank you for it.” Alessandra laughed, sharp. “He’s my old acquaintance. He means I’m generous.” Ben felt his face heat. “I’m not — I’m fine.” Marco leaned in, quieter. “She doesn’t mean anything. She collects moments. Don’t get collected.” Alessandra stood, tossing coins on the table. “Come on, Professor. You’re missing the good part.” ### The good part was a rooftop no one was supposed to be on. She’d known a custodian, she said, and they climbed a fire escape behind a laundry. Rome opened up below them, gold and terracotta. Ben sat on the ledge, knees to his chest. “This is… illegal.” “Everything good is,” she said. She was barefoot, the Vespa keys jingling in her pocket. She pulled out the sugar packet, the blue beads, the cherry stem, laid them on the ledge like a tiny still life. “You’re a magpie,” he said softly. She looked at him, really looked. “You’re not scared.” “I’m terrified,” he admitted. “I haven’t been terrified since my viva.” She smiled, not the sharp one from the morning. “Good.” The wind lifted her hair. For a moment neither moved. Then her phone buzzed. She glanced at it, sighed. “I have to go. Delivery.” Ben stood too fast. “Already? It’s only —” “It’s always only,” she said. “You’ll be okay. You have your guidebook.” He didn’t want to let her go. “Will I see you again?” She swung her leg over the imaginary Vespa. “If you’re lucky, I’ll run you over again.” She kissed him this time, properly, quick and warm, and was gone down the fire escape before he could apologize. Ben stayed on the roof until the sun bled out over the Tiber, clutching a stolen cherry stem in his fist, utterly disoriented, and completely, stupidly smitten.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt's requirements. The author successfully creates the requested interconnected scenes spanning a single day in Rome, establishing clear character contrasts between the impulsive Italian courier Alessandra and the reserved British academic Ben. The narrative structure works well, using brief vignettes connected by location and escalating intimacy. The characterization is particularly effective. Alessandra emerges as a compelling figure - her kleptomania is subtly woven throughout (sugar packet, cherry, beads) without heavy-handed exposition. Her dialogue crackles with personality ("On sabbatical from common sense"), and her actions feel authentic to someone who lives on the edge. Ben's transformation from bumbling academic to willing participant feels earned through the progression of scenes, though it borders on being slightly rushed. The prose style is confident and economical. Sentences like "The Trevi Fountain was already sweating at nine in the morning" immediately establish atmosphere and voice. The author demonstrates skill in sensory details - the Vespa smelling of "gasoline and citrus," the tactile experience of Rome's narrow streets. The dialogue feels natural and reveals character effectively, particularly Alessandra's rapid-fire delivery contrasted with Ben's hesitant formality. The inclusion of Marco as a warning voice adds complexity and foreshadowing without being heavy-handed. His brief appearance serves multiple functions - establishing Alessandra's history, creating tension, and giving Ben (and readers) pause about her intentions. However, the piece has some limitations. While the chemistry between the characters is palpable, Ben's complete transformation from cautious academic to smitten risk-taker happens quite rapidly. The ending, while romantically satisfying, leans toward the predictable - the mysterious woman disappearing after a perfect day, leaving the man transformed. The kleptomania subplot, while well-executed, could have been developed with more psychological complexity. The writing occasionally veers toward overly polished territory, with some moments feeling slightly constructed rather than organic. The rooftop scene, while beautiful, edges toward romantic cliché. The final image of Ben clutching the cherry stem is effective but somewhat expected. Overall, this is accomplished writing that fulfills its brief effectively. The author demonstrates strong control over pacing, character voice, and atmospheric detail. While not groundbreaking, it's engaging and well-crafted contemporary romance writing. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I’m wiping the same spot on the bar with a rag as I listen. It’s the chipped corner by the synth-ice machine where everyone leans. The rag is damp and smells like cheap citrus cleaner and Vega whisky. The Last Outpost hums. The miners are playing low-stakes sabacc at table three, Jax is complaining about his ex again, and Mara is trying to convince a cargo hauler that her “hand-picked” moon grapes are not, in fact, fermented in his coolant tank. Cozy. Safe. My kind of chaos. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” I look up. He’s already plopped down on the stool at the end, where the light doesn’t quite reach. Tentacled dreads, askew, half tucked behind one ear, half dripping onto his collar. Skin the color of old bruises. Eyes too wide. He smells like ozone and bad decisions. I keep wiping the same spot. “You’re new,” I say. He doesn’t look at me. He looks at the bottle. “You’re Nettle.” “Nets to my friends.” “Nets,” he says. “Good. I need you to not be a friend for a minute.” I pour. The Vega is amber and expensive. I pour a double anyway. I set it down. He doesn’t touch it. “You’re shaking,” I say. “I’m frazzled,” he says. “That’s different.” “Right.” I wipe the same spot. “What’s your name?” He finally looks at me. “Doesn’t matter. It won’t be tomorrow.” “Okay.” I lean on the bar. “That’s ominous. You want a coaster?” “I want you to listen. And then I want you to pretend you didn’t.” The miners laugh. Jax says something about Mara’s grapes. I nod like I’m listening. “I’m here about the Outpost,” he says, quiet. “Specifically, about you.” My rag stills for half a second. Then I start again on the same spot. “You don’t know me.” “I know you were a compliance auditor for Helion Dynamics,” he says. “Sector Nine. You signed off on the Kessari evacuation waiver. You quit three months later and you never filed a final report.” The bar is suddenly too loud. I keep wiping. “People talk,” I say. “People remember,” he says. “I remember because I was on that evac team. My sister was on that list. You signed her out.” I pour myself a finger of Vega, which is against house rules. I don’t drink on shift. I drink now. “Her name was Lira,” he says. “She was seven. Tentacled dreads like mine. She had a birthmark shaped like a comet. You signed the waiver that said the evac ship was safe. It wasn’t.” I set the glass down. “I signed what I was told to sign.” “No,” he says. “You signed what you were paid to sign. And then you ran.” The rag is damp through. I’m just rubbing now. “Why are you telling me this?” I ask. “Because the Consortium is coming for the Outpost,” he says. “Tomorrow, 0400. They have a warrant for a Helion defector. They’re not naming names yet, but they’re going to sweep. They’ll lock down the airlocks, scan every registry, every chip, every body.” “Why tell me?” “Because I’m carrying a data core,” he says. “It’s in my pack. It’s the full Kessari evacuation logs. Names, signatures, payout records, the doctored safety reports. You’re on it. A lot of people are on it. If that core gets to the Belt Authority, Helion falls. If Helion falls, a lot of people get paid. Or a lot of people get dead.” He finally picks up the whisky. Doesn’t drink. “I need a place to put it,” he says. “Somewhere they won’t find it in a sweep. Somewhere they won’t think to look.” I wipe the same spot. The wood is warm under my palm. “You want me to hide it for you,” I say. “I want you to hide it for my sister,” he says. “I want you to decide if you’re still the person who signed that waiver, or if you’re the person who bartends at a lazy hub in an asteroid belt because you’re trying to be better.” Mara comes up to the bar. “Nets, love, can you tell this hauler his grapes are fine? He’s crying.” “Give me five,” I say. She frowns. “You’re wiping the same spot.” “It’s a good spot,” I say. She leaves. The stranger watches me. “You don’t have to say yes.” “I don’t have to say no,” I say. He slides a small, dented case across the bar. It’s warm. “It’s not heavy. It’s not big. It’s just… evidence.” I don’t touch it. I keep wiping the same spot on the bar counter with a rag as I listen. “The Outpost has rules,” I say. “No contraband. No politics. No Helion.” “The Outpost has you,” he says. “And you have a past you’re trying to keep in equilibrium with your talents. That’s what you told Jax last week when he asked why you never take the off-station jobs.” I hate that he’s right. “If I say yes,” I say, “you’ll be gone by morning. And if the Consortium comes, I’ll be the one who hid it.” “If I say no,” he says, “the core goes to a dead drop on the outer ring. They’ll find it in an hour. They’ll find you in a day.” The sabacc game cheers. Jax kisses Mara’s cheek. The Outpost keeps humming like it’s safe. I look at the case. I look at his tentacled dreads, askew and wet. I look at my rag, which has gone gray. “Vega whisky, neat,” I say, because it’s what he asked for and I’m still a bartender. “You didn’t drink it.” “I’m saving it,” he says. “For after.” I don’t answer. I just keep wiping the same spot.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements, delivering approximately 1000 words in first-person present tense with roughly 60% dialogue as requested. The author establishes the cozy sci-fi atmosphere of The Last Outpost effectively, creating a lived-in space with authentic background characters and activities. The central conflict is well-constructed and appropriately unresolved. The stranger's revelation about Nets' past as a compliance auditor who signed off on a faulty evacuation creates genuine moral tension. The approaching Consortium sweep adds urgency without feeling contrived. The author skillfully avoids resolving this conflict within the chapter, leaving Nets at a crossroads between self-preservation and redemption. Character work is particularly strong. Nets feels authentic as someone trying to escape her past while maintaining the delicate social ecosystem of the bar. Her nervous habit of wiping the same spot becomes an effective physical manifestation of her internal state. The stranger is compelling in his quiet desperation, and his personal connection to Nets' past decisions adds emotional weight. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and maintaining the bar's atmosphere. Conversations flow organically, from Mara's interruption about the grapes to Jax's background complaints. The stranger's measured delivery of devastating information contrasts effectively with the casual bar chatter. The prose maintains consistent voice throughout, balancing the cozy atmosphere with underlying tension. Descriptive elements like "skin the color of old bruises" and "smells like ozone and bad decisions" create vivid impressions without becoming overwrought. The repetitive motif of wiping the same spot works as both character detail and structural element. The world-building feels authentic to the cozy sci-fi genre - advanced enough to feel futuristic but grounded enough to feel familiar. References to sabacc games, moon grapes, and various alien characteristics integrate naturally without exposition dumps. Some minor weaknesses include occasional repetitive phrasing and a few moments where the tension could be tighter. The ending, while appropriately unresolved, might benefit from slightly more internal conflict from Nets. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise well-crafted piece that successfully establishes character, conflict, and atmosphere while maintaining genre expectations. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder. It’s been doing that since I got dumped on Canal Street at 2 a.m. last night, which is probably a sign. Or just cheap fabric. I keep yanking it back up and it slides right down again like it’s trying to get away from me. I’m standing under the neon of a closed pawn shop and I’m trying to decide if I’m cold or just shaking. Both. New Orleans is humid in a way Tennessee never was. It sticks to the back of my neck. My hoodie is too thin and my jeans are too heavy and my sneakers are soaked from when I tried to sleep in the bus station bathroom and woke up when someone kicked the door. I walked. That’s what I do now. Walk. I walked from the bus station to the river because the bus station felt like a trap. I walked past people who were still out at 6 a.m. drinking coffee like it was normal. I walked past a guy in a Saints jersey who asked if I needed help and I said no because the last person who offered help was the guy who picked me up in Memphis and then decided he didn’t want a “troubled kid” in his car anymore. He pulled over at the first light downtown and said “I can’t do this” and I just nodded because I didn’t want to cry in front of him. Two days ago I told my mom I’m trans. That’s the real deal. Not invented drama. I practiced it for months in the shower. I said it out loud in the mirror. I came out at dinner and my dad went quiet and my mom started crying and then the school counselor called and used the phrase “concerning behavioural patterns” and I heard it from the kitchen. That’s when I knew I wasn’t staying. I didn’t have a plan. I had thirty minutes. I packed a hoodie, my sketchbook, a toothbrush, $87 from the jar I’d been stealing from for six months, and my phone which is now at 12%. I’m not supposed to be here. I’m supposed to be in school. A bell jingles and I jerk. The strap slips again. The coffee shop across the street just opened. The sign says BEIGNETS. I have $87. I can’t afford to be hungry and I can’t afford to be seen. I sit on the curb and eat the granola bar I stole from the gas station. It tastes like cardboard. “Hey, you look lost.” I look up. A kid is standing over me. Not a kid-kid. Maybe 18, 19. Shaved head, nose ring, a faded tour shirt for a band I don’t know. They have a duffel bag that looks like it’s been through a war. They’re holding two coffees. “I’m not lost,” I say, because that’s what you say. “You’re sitting on the sidewalk in front of a closed pawn shop at seven in the morning with a backpack that won’t stay on. That’s lost.” They crouch down. “I’m Ren.” I don’t give my name. I learned that on the road. “Okay.” They hand me a coffee anyway. It’s hot. My hands are shaking so bad I almost spill it. “You’re new,” they say. Not a question. “Two states away,” I say. “From Tennessee.” Ren nods like that means something. “First day?” I nod. They sit on the curb next to me, careful not to touch. “First day sucks. Second day sucks less. Third day you either find a spot or you get picked up.” I think about my mom’s voice on the phone last night. Did she call? I turned my phone off. “I don’t want to get picked up.” “Nobody does.” Ren takes a sip. “You got a place?” “No.” “Yeah.” They tap their duffel. “Me neither. I’m crashing at a friend’s couch tonight but the couch is conditional. You want to walk with me for a bit? I know where the water fountains that actually work are.” I want to say no. I want to say yes. The strap slips. I fix it. “Okay,” I say. We walk. Ren tells me about the Quarter, about which alleys to avoid after dark, about the guy who sells fake IDs out of a laundromat on St. Claude. They don’t ask where I’m from or why I’m here. That’s good. That’s really good. At a corner with a mural of a brass band, Ren stops. “You hungry?” “I ate a granola bar.” “That’s not food.” They pull a paper bag from their duffel. Inside are two day-old po’boys from somewhere. “I was gonna eat this later. You can have half.” I stare at it. “I can’t—” “You can. I’m not a charity case. I’m just not hungry right now.” I take it. It’s cold but it’s real food. We sit on a bench while the city wakes up around us. Tourists with big cameras. Street musicians tuning. A woman in a nurse’s scrubs walks by and gives Ren a small nod like they know each other. “You’re trans too?” I ask before I can stop myself. Ren shrugs. “Yeah. You?” I feel my face go hot. “Yeah.” They don’t say anything judgmental. They just say, “It’s harder out here than people think. Everyone wants a story.” I think about the school counselor. The smug voice. Concerning behavioural patterns. I think about my dad saying “we need to talk about this” like I’m a problem to solve. “I told my family,” I say. My voice cracks. “It went bad.” Ren nods. “Mine too. Mine kicked me out when I was fifteen. I’ve been bouncing since.” We sit in silence for a minute. The strap slips off my shoulder again and I don’t fix it right away. I just let it hang. “Do you trust people?” I ask. Ren laughs, short and not mean. “No. I trust patterns. You’re not gonna rob me. I’m not gonna rob you. That’s a pattern.” “I don’t know what the dangers are.” “There are a lot. Men in cars. People who offer you a shower. People who are too nice.” Ren looks at me. “Don’t take rides from strangers. Don’t sleep in doorways on Bourbon. Don’t let anyone touch your bag.” My bag. The strap keeps slipping. “I have $87,” I whisper. Ren doesn’t flinch. “Keep it on you, not in the bag. Split it up.” I nod. I feel like I’m learning a language I never wanted to learn. We walk a little more. Ren shows me a library with bathrooms you can use without a card. A 24-hour laundromat with outlets. A bench under a tree where the cops don’t bother you. At noon the sun is brutal. Ren stands up, brushes off their jeans. “I gotta go work a shift. Bar back on Frenchmen. You can come if you want. Cash under the table, no questions.” I think about my mom. I think about the bus station. I think about the strap slipping. “I don’t have ID,” I say. “Most people don’t.” I don’t say yes. I don’t say no. I just watch them walk away, duffel slung over one shoulder, not slipping. I’m still on the bench. My backpack is at my feet now because the strap finally gave up. I’m two states away, I’m hungry, I’m scared, and for the first time in 48 hours I’m not alone with it. That’s a dangerous feeling.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Taylor's voice as a 16-year-old trans runaway navigating their first day in New Orleans. The first-person mixed tense narration works effectively, blending present observations with recent past events. The author creates a believable street-level perspective of survival, incorporating practical details like working water fountains, safe sleeping spots, and the economics of being homeless. The characterization of Taylor feels authentic - their vulnerability, wariness, and conflicted emotions ring true for someone in their situation. The internal monologue effectively conveys the overwhelming nature of their circumstances while maintaining the character's resilience. Ren serves as an effective foil, providing street wisdom without falling into mentor clichés. Their dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing plot, revealing character, and providing exposition about survival tactics. The recurring motif of the slipping backpack strap works well as both a practical detail and metaphor for Taylor's precarious situation. The prose maintains an appropriate rawness that matches the subject matter without becoming overwrought. Sensory details like the humidity, the taste of cardboard granola bars, and the physical sensations of exhaustion ground the reader in Taylor's experience. The emotional complexity is well-handled - Taylor's fear, loneliness, and desperate hope are layered throughout without becoming melodramatic. The piece avoids easy answers or unearned optimism while still providing moments of human connection that feel genuine rather than contrived. Some minor weaknesses include occasional repetitive phrasing and a few moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly expository. The pacing occasionally slows during descriptive passages, though this generally serves the contemplative mood. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely hopeful nor gratuitously dark. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The problem with having an Apocalypse Buddy is that you are never quite sure if you are the protagonist or the sidekick. Midas was fairly sure he was the protagonist, mainly because he was the only one who bled. He sat on an upturned milk crate in what had once been the pantry of a house and was now home base, which is a generous term for a room with a working door and a roof that only leaked in the spirit of the thing. Chewy sat on the table beside him. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from some long-forgotten before time, approximately the size of a small child and approximately as useful. He had been rescued from a ruined toy store in the Year of the Quiet Sirens and had since developed a personality best described as 'enthusiastic corporate ghost'. "Right," said Midas, consulting a scrap of paper on which he had written WATER in capital letters and then, underneath, in smaller, less hopeful letters, maybe also food. Chewy blinked his glass eyes and emitted a soft whir. "Buy One Get One Free!" he announced cheerfully. Midas had learned not to ask. "The cistern's down to the last three inches," Midas said. "And the rain hasn't come since the Month of Ash. The old mall has those big water tanks on the roof. If we can get up there, we can siphon." Chewy considered this with the gravity of a stuffed animal who had once been programmed to sell cereal. "The future is now!" he said. "Yes," said Midas. "And the present is thirsty." It was a sound plan. Sound plans are the ones that go sideways with the most enthusiasm. The mall was three miles out across the scrub. It used to be called The Galleria. Now it was The Gallery, because everything there was on display and nobody was buying. Midas went in the front door, which was now a very large mouth with its teeth knocked out. Chewy came along because Chewy always came along, and because Midas had once tried to leave him and Chewy had rolled under the porch and started saying "Limited Time Offer!" for six hours straight until Midas relented. The interior was a cathedral of dead fluorescent light. Pigeons had taken up residence in the food court. A feral cat colony ran a protection racket out of the old Hot Topic. Midas negotiated this by offering a half a biscuit and a promise not to look them in the eye. The stairs to the roof were blocked by a fallen escalator, which was a reasonable metaphor for late capitalism. Midas climbed. Halfway up, Chewy's chest panel popped open with a sigh of ancient pneumatics. "Have you tried... new... cola?" he said. "Not now, Chewy." "New cola!" Chewy insisted, and then, with the dignity of a machine, fell silent. At the top of the stairs, the roof was a landscape of rust and tar. The tanks were there, two great blue whales beached in the sun. The first was dry as a sermon. The second had a trickle. Midas set up the siphon, a length of hose he had liberated from a garden centre in the Year of the Quiet Sirens. It took a while. It always took a while. While he waited, he sat on the tank's lip and watched the world. From up here you could see the whole of the collapse, which was mostly brown and occasionally a stubborn green. Chewy rolled to the edge and looked out. "Two for one!" he said. That was when the roof gave a little sigh of its own. The old mall had been built cheaply and had been standing for a long time. It decided, with the quiet dignity of a building, that it was tired. A panel of tar and gravel shifted under Chewy's weight. Chewy, being animo-tronic, did not have weight so much as the illusion of it, but the roof had not been consulted on this. Chewy went down. Midas lunged. He caught one floppy ear. The rest of Chewy went over the edge with a cheerful "Act Now!" and disappeared into the service alley below. Midas was left hanging by one hand from the tank's lip, with a siphon hose in his mouth and a koala in free fall. He made a choice that historians would later call brave and engineers would call stupid. He let go. He landed in a pile of shopping trolleys that had been there since before the collapse and which had, over the years, become a kind of soft furniture. He was bruised, dusty, and his left boot was now permanently attached to a trolley. Chewy had landed better. He had landed in a nest of feral cats who, it turned out, had a deep respect for plush toys with moving parts. They were inspecting him with the solemnity of scholars. One of them was trying to bat his arm. Midas retrieved Chewy. Chewy was scuffed, one eye hanging by a thread, and his battery pack was leaking a smell like old pennies. He still worked. "Your mission... is... clear!" Chewy said proudly. "I think my mission is to stop falling," Midas said. They had no water. The siphon hose was still up on the roof, now slowly draining the last of the tank onto the concrete. Midas looked at the hose, looked at the alley, looked at the three miles of scrub back to home base. "Alternative plan," he said. They went home. Midas went home first, on foot, limping, with Chewy clutched to his chest like a very ungrateful child. The feral cats followed for a while, then lost interest. A crow picked up Midas's hat and flew off with it. Midas did not chase it. He had learned that some losses are not worth the calories. Chewy went home second, and by a different route entirely. About a mile from the house, Chewy's battery finally gave up the ghost with a sad little *pfft* and he went limp. Midas set him down to rest. While he was resting, a gust of wind caught the lightweight plastic of Chewy's body and rolled him down the embankment. He tumbled through brambles, over a fence, and came to rest in the garden of the house next door, where a boy who had been collecting bottle caps for a trade stared at him in wonder. "Cool," the boy said, and picked him up. Midas arrived home base an hour later, covered in trolley rust, with no water, and with a very distinct lack of koala. He sat on the milk crate and waited. Chewy arrived at dusk, carried by the boy who had found him, who was now calling him Mr. Koala and who wanted to trade him for a can of beans. Midas gave him the can of beans. Chewy was returned to the table, scuffed, one eye dangling, and with a small tuft of bramble in his ear. He powered up on the boy's spare battery, a thing Midas had not known the boy possessed. "Satisfaction guaranteed!" Chewy said. Midas looked at the empty cistern, at his bruised knees, at Chewy who was now missing a foot and smelling faintly of cat. "Well," he said. "Tomorrow we can try the water tower." Chewy blinked. "Buy now!" Midas sighed. It was, in its own way, a perfect plan.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, philosophical observations, and ability to find profound meaning in absurd situations. The opening line immediately establishes the Pratchettesque tone with its wry observation about protagonist versus sidekick dynamics, and this voice remains consistent throughout. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believable post-apocalyptic survivor - pragmatic, resigned to his circumstances, yet retaining enough humanity to care for his malfunctioning companion. Chewy, despite being an animatronic toy, becomes genuinely endearing through his corporate catchphrases that serve as a haunting echo of consumer culture. The relationship between them feels authentic and touching without being sentimental. The plot structure follows the prompt requirements well - deliberation, mission planning, inevitable complications, and return home worse for wear. The mission's failure feels organic rather than forced, arising naturally from the deteriorated infrastructure and the characters' limitations. The writing shows rather than tells, allowing readers to understand the world through concrete details like the "cathedral of dead fluorescent light" and the feral cats running a "protection racket." The prose is elegant and controlled, with memorable phrases like "the future is now, and the present is thirsty" that capture both humor and pathos. The pacing moves smoothly from setup through action to resolution, maintaining reader engagement throughout. The dialogue, while limited, serves its purpose effectively, particularly Chewy's corporate speak which becomes increasingly poignant as commentary on lost civilization. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - they've failed their mission but found an unexpected solution through community connection (the boy with bottle caps). This feels earned rather than artificially positive, maintaining the story's realistic tone while offering a glimmer of hope. The final exchange suggests they'll continue their quixotic adventures, which feels true to both characters. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the Pratchett pastiche becomes slightly obvious, and a few descriptions that edge toward being overly clever. However, these don't significantly detract from what is overall a well-crafted piece that successfully fulfills its ambitious stylistic goals. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door of *Llyfrau Llandeilo* jingled and the rain came in with him. Elin didn’t look up from the till. “We’re closed.” “We’re not,” the man said, shaking water off a black bomber jacket. He was tall enough that he had to duck under the low doorway, and he was holding his phone like it was a live thing. “The sign says open till six. It’s five-forty-two.” Elin looked up then. He was dripping onto her secondhand carpet, and the paparazzi were out there on the High Street with their umbrellas and their long lenses, shouting his name. She knew it even if she pretended she didn’t. Finn Calloway. The poster for *The Kings of Ash* had been in the window for a month. “Right,” she said. “You’re trespassing then.” He grinned, helplessly charming, and tried to make it a joke. “Only if you press charges, love. And you look too tired for paperwork.” She went back to ringing up a paperback. “I’m always tired.” “Fair. I’m always famous. It’s a terrible trade.” He peeled off his jacket, revealing a white t-shirt underneath. He was shaking. “They’ve been on me since the hotel. I just wanted a loo. And a moment where nobody knows my arse from my elbow.” Elin finally looked at him properly. He had that rogue thing about him, all easy smile and messy hair, like he was letting you in on a secret. It was a practiced look. She’d seen it on interviews. “You could have used the hotel loo.” “My driver’s a coward. He left me. Said he had a family.” He leaned against the poetry shelf, careful not to touch anything. “You’re Elin, aren’t you? The owner. I asked about you at the café. They said you’re the only person in town who won’t take a selfie.” “That’s because I don’t own a phone that takes selfies.” He laughed, delighted. “See? I told them you were formidable.” “I’m busy.” “Of course you are. Forgive me.” He held up his hands. “I’m not here to be a nuisance. I’m here to hide. Five minutes. I promise I won’t sign anything.” She glanced at the window. A flash went off. “You’ll be fine. They’ll get bored.” “They never get bored.” He lowered his voice, conspiratorial. “They’ll wait until I buy a Welsh cake and then they’ll have the shot.” Elin snorted despite herself. “You’re not buying a Welsh cake.” “I was hoping you’d sell me one.” “I don’t sell Welsh cakes.” He looked wounded, theatrical. “You’re breaking my heart.” She reached under the counter and pulled out a battered field guide. *Birds of Wales*. The spine was cracked. “You’re standing in front of the choughs.” He blinked. “Sorry?” “The book. You’re blocking it.” He stepped aside, then picked it up. “You keep this?” “Of course I do. People ask.” “Do they?” He opened it carefully. Inside, in neat pencil, were ticks and dates. *Cwm Elan, 12.03. Choughs, 3.* “You bird.” “I walk.” “You birdwatch.” He said it like a revelation. “I birdwatch.” Elin’s mouth twitched. “You’re joking.” “I’m deadly serious.” He flipped a page. “See? You’ve got the red-billed chough here. I saw a pair last week on the cliff path near Aberporth. I wrote it down.” He tapped his chest. “In my head. Because my phone’s dead and my publicist would have a stroke if she knew I was looking at birds instead of doing press.” She stared at him. “You’re Finn Calloway.” “I’m Finn, yes. And I’m a terrible actor when I’m not acting.” He was talking too fast now, trying to fill the silence. “Do you hate me? Be honest. I can take it. I’ve been told I’m insufferable. That I’m a diva. That I cry in trailers. All true.” “I don’t know you.” “Exactly! You don’t know me. That’s refreshing. Everyone likes me. Or pretends to. It’s exhausting.” The charm slipped for a second, and the boy underneath showed. “I need people to like me, Elin. It’s pathetic, I know.” She felt flustered and didn’t know why. He was still dripping. “You’re wet.” “I know.” “Dry yourself.” She pointed to a tea towel behind the counter. “And don’t touch the books.” He did, obediently, and his shoulders dropped. “Thank you.” She shouldn’t have liked the way he said it. She shouldn’t have liked the way he looked at the field guide like it was a script. “You do the choughs?” he asked, quieter now. “Every spring. They come back to the quarry. I’ve been logging them since I was sixteen. My dad had the binoculars.” He pulled a pair of battered Zeiss from his jacket pocket. “Mine too. He taught me on the coast in Cornwall. I still have his notebook. I bring it everywhere. It’s embarrassing.” “You’re embarrassed by birds?” “I’m embarrassed by being liked for the wrong things.” He smiled, smaller this time. Not the rogue smile. The real one. “You’re not going to ask for a selfie, are you?” “No.” He sighed with relief. “Thank God. I’m really not good at that.” The rain eased. A photographer shouted his name again, muffled by glass. “You should go,” Elin said. “In a minute.” He didn’t move. “Can I ask you something? If I come back tomorrow, when you’re actually open, will you tell me where the best spot is? For the choughs. Honestly.” She should have said no. She should have told him to get a guidebook like everyone else. “South of the quarry,” she said. “Past the old lime kiln. Go at dawn. Don’t wear bright colours.” He wrote it down on the back of a receipt. “Elin. Thank you.” She busied herself with the till. “You’re welcome.” He hesitated at the door, jacket back on. “You’re not immune, you know. You’re just good at pretending.” She didn’t look up. “I’m busy.” He laughed, that easy rogue laugh again, but his eyes stayed on her a beat too long. “I’ll let you get back to it.” The bell jingled as he left. The paparazzi surged. Elin watched him duck out into the rain, and only when the door shut did she realize her hand was still trembling around the field guide.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a Welsh bookstore setting with authentic details like "Llyfrau Llandeilo" and establishes the paparazzi chase scenario convincingly. The dialogue-driven approach works well, with each character maintaining distinct voices throughout - Elin's terse, practical responses contrasting effectively with Finn's more verbose, charm-laden speech patterns. The characterization hits the brief accurately. Finn emerges as the requested rogue with fragile ego, desperately needing validation ("I need people to like me, Elin. It's pathetic, I know") while deploying practiced charm that occasionally slips to reveal vulnerability. Elin maintains her surface immunity while showing subtle signs of being affected, particularly in moments like her hand trembling at the end. The birdwatching detail serves as an effective bridge between the characters, providing genuine common ground that allows Finn's charm offensive to falter into something more authentic. This shared interest feels organic rather than contrived, and creates a believable basis for connection beyond his celebrity status. The prose maintains consistent quality without becoming overwrought. Descriptions are economical but evocative - "dripping onto her secondhand carpet" and "the boy underneath showed" effectively convey atmosphere and character revelation. The Welsh setting feels authentic without being heavy-handed. However, the piece suffers from some predictable beats. The celebrity-hiding-from-paparazzi setup, while well-executed, follows familiar romance tropes. The birdwatching connection, though handled skillfully, provides a somewhat convenient shared interest. The ending, with Elin's trembling hand, telegraphs her attraction rather obviously. The emotional complexity could be deeper. While both characters show surface versus depth, their internal conflicts remain relatively straightforward. Finn's need for validation and Elin's guarded nature are clearly established but not explored with particular nuance. The dialogue occasionally veers toward exposition, particularly when Finn explains his birdwatching hobby, though this serves the plot necessity of establishing connection. Some exchanges feel slightly constructed to advance the romantic tension rather than emerging purely from character. The pacing works well within the scene's constraints, building from initial antagonism through grudging respect to mutual attraction. The author manages the chemistry effectively without rushing the development or making the attraction feel unearned. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave with a sigh rather than a creak. Aya had expected iron and a trap. Instead the underhold exhaled cold air that smelled of brine, old whale-oil and damp stone. The gas lamps along the vaulted throat of the guild’s underhold burned low, their mantles sputtering yellow over black iron ribs. The quiet was wrong. Above, the Morska had been a riot of whispers and running boots after the raid, men shouting about the Harbormaster’s arrest, about the lock on the scythan vault being changed. Down here there was no one. Simeon’s pocket watch ticked loudly in his waistcoat pocket. Each second struck the hollow of the chamber and Aya counted them against her pulse. “Too quiet,” Katra murmured, hand at the hilt of her stiletto. She was all lean muscle and street, her mask a strip of soot-stained linen. “It’s a snare.” “It’s an opportunity,” Aya said, and the lie steadied her own hand on the iron ring. She had spent three months learning the guild’s routes by rote, by bribe, by the careful way she could pull a thin thread of immateria from the air and make a lock forget its tumblers. She had risen because she was useful and because no one looked twice at a girl who smiled politely and never asked questions. Now the Harbormaster was in chains, the vault was unguarded, and the artifact waited. She pushed the door. The underhold opened into a circular chamber sunk deep beneath the wharf. A scythan reliquary, a black basalt sarcophagus ringed with brass, sat on a dais at the centre. And in front of it stood a woman. Aya’s breath caught. It was Varga. The Harbormaster. The woman the broadsheets had printed with a wanted notice this morning, the woman the watch said they had taken at dawn in a bloodless raid on the Salt Row. She was unshackled, her coat still damp from the river, a brass derringer glinting at her hip and two of her bone-carved bodyguards flanking her like statues. Her face was a map of old cuts and older authority. “Close the door,” Varga said softly. Simeon moved first, not to fight but to step between them. The watch ticked. “Madame, we were told—” “You were told a great many things,” Varga said. “That I was in the cells. That the vault was open. That a new hand could take the seat.” She looked past Simeon to Aya, and her eyes narrowed. “You. The rat who’s been opening my locks for six weeks.” Aya’s gloved fingers tightened on the doorframe. The mask she wore, a thin porcelain half-mask painted with a gull, suddenly felt too hot. “Hands where I can see them,” one of the bodyguards said, and the steel of his truncheon caught the lamplight. Katra laughed, a short, sharp sound. “You’ve got the wrong end of the night, Harbormaster. We’re here for the scythan—” “You’re here for me,” Varga said. “I sent the message about my arrest myself. I sent the men to Salt Row with my own coat and my own cuff. I wanted to see who would come down here when the rats thought the cat was dead.” The pocket watch ticked. Aya’s internal voice, the one that sounded like her mother in the attic with a candle, whispered: *You should have stayed in the ballroom.* Varga’s gaze never left Aya. “Take the mask off.” Aya hesitated. The mask was the only wall between her and the world of carriages and calling cards and the quiet, polite horror of the aristocracy. If it came off, the guild would know. If the guild knew, the city would know. If the city knew, the name of the hanged woman would be spoken again in her own mouth. Simeon’s watch ticked again, loud as a hammer. “Do it,” Varga said, not unkindly. “I’m tired of guessing.” Aya lifted her hands. The porcelain came away with a soft click. Her hair, dark and unbound beneath the cap, fell forward. The gaslight caught the pale, familiar curve of her cheek. Varga’s expression did not change. “Lady Aya Varnholt.” Katra swore under her breath. Simeon went very still. *Oh God. Oh Mother.* Aya felt the old familiar cold coil in her stomach, the same cold that had been in the courtyard when the rope was put around her mother’s neck for summoning. Immateria was feared and barely understood, and men trusted brass and oil and steel. A woman who could call things from the dark was a contagion. “You’re a Varnholt,” Varga said. “You’re also the girl who lifted the ledger from my own office last month without tripping a single ward. I wondered why the wards were so polite.” Aya forced her voice level. “I can be useful.” “You can be dead,” Varga said. “You and your friends. You tried to take the heart of my guild in my own house while I was supposedly in chains. That’s a hanging offense in the Morska, and a worse one in the city.” The bodyguards stepped closer. Simeon’s hands were already empty, raised. Katra’s stiletto was in the guard’s grip. The watch ticked. Aya felt the immateria stir at the edge of her thoughts, a thin, hungry draft. She could pull it, she could— No. Not here. Not with Varga watching. “Wait,” Aya said, and the word came out thinner than she wanted. “You don’t want to kill me.” Varga tilted her head. “Why not?” “Because I’m a hostage worth more than a corpse.” Aya swallowed. The words tasted like ash. “My father sits on the Admiralty Board. He funds the wharf patrols. He funds the new whale-oil refineries. If I disappear tonight, the questions will start. If I disappear in a way that ties to the Morska, the questions will become a raid. A real one.” She was bargaining with her own ruin. If Varga kept her, the mask would be gone forever. The aristocracy would learn that Lady Aya Varnholt consorted with thieves, with immateria, with the guild that had killed her mother’s name. The noose would be metaphorical, but no less real. Simeon’s watch ticked. “She’s right,” he said quickly. “The girl’s a name. A name buys time.” Varga studied her as if weighing a coin. The lamplight made shadows under her eyes. “You’re also a witch,” she said quietly. “I can smell it on you, girl. The air goes thin around you when you’re nervous.” Aya’s throat closed. “I’m a scientist,” she said, the lie she told at parties. “My mother—” “Your mother was hanged for less than you’ve done in this hall,” Varga said. “You think I don’t know what immateria does to a house? It eats the plaster. It makes the men in it hear things in the pipes.” Katra made a small, helpless sound. “Madame, we didn’t know you were—” “I know,” Varga said. “Now you do too.” She lifted the derringer, not pointing it, just holding it. “You will come with me. All three of you. You will be quiet. You will be useful. And you, Lady Varnholt, will learn what it costs to play in a guild that does not care for your pedigree or your pretty magicks.” The watch ticked again, marking the second Aya’s life split into before and after the mask. She nodded, because the alternative was steel, and because the quiet of the underhold was suddenly, terribly full.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the "whalepunk" fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a vivid Victorian-gothic atmosphere through sensory details like "brine, old whale-oil and damp stone" and the recurring motif of Simeon's pocket watch marking tension. The dialogue feels authentic to the period and setting, with characters speaking in appropriately formal yet gritty tones. The story adheres well to the prompt's requirements, hitting all major story beats: the trio enters the underhold, discovers the supposedly imprisoned guild leader, Aya is unmasked and captured, and she attempts to negotiate using her aristocratic value as leverage. The author skillfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension and power dynamics. Character motivations feel believable throughout. Varga's elaborate trap demonstrates cunning leadership, while Aya's internal conflict between her aristocratic identity and criminal activities creates compelling emotional complexity. Her desperation when bargaining with her own social ruin feels authentic and earned. The prose maintains consistent quality without becoming overwrought or purple. Descriptive passages like the scythan reliquary and the underhold's architecture effectively establish mood without excessive ornamentation. The recurring watch motif provides effective structural rhythm. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "too quiet" setup telegraphs the trap somewhat obviously, and Varga's revelation follows familiar patterns. The piece also relies heavily on exposition in places, particularly when establishing Aya's magical abilities and family history. The dialogue serves multiple functions effectively, revealing character relationships, advancing plot, and maintaining period authenticity. Varga's measured threats and Aya's desperate bargaining feel particularly well-crafted. The emotional complexity around Aya's dual identity and the weight of her mother's execution adds depth beyond simple adventure plotting. The ending appropriately dark and uncertain, matching the gothic tone without forced positivity.
