+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan listened to it the way he listened to a pump in a mine shaft — for changes in pitch that meant trouble. The drone never changed. That was the trouble. He sat strapped into a jump seat bolted to the bulkhead of the Antares shuttle *Harrow*. The cabin smelled of recycled air and hot plastic. Through the small porthole, Mars was already a thin copper line, and beyond it the black was absolute. He had left his plot, his half-built hab, his survey rig, and the vein that had made him a problem in less than six hours. They had come at dawn. Four men in grey fatigues, polite, with rifles slung but hands visible. The insignia on their collars was a stylized star over an open hand — Antares Diplomatic Corps. Diplomatic in name only. The corporal had smiled while he read the writ. “Mr. Neegan, you are requested to attend a consultation off-world. It is not an arrest. It is an invitation. You will be returned.” Arthur had asked who requested it. The corporal had said, “The party will introduce itself.” Now the party was waiting. The *Harrow* docked with a soft thump and a sigh of equalizing pressure. A steward in a blue tunic unbuckled Arthur and escorted him down a narrow corridor lit by amber strips. The walls were lined with old-fashioned brass plaques naming donors to the Antares Colonization Fund, 2198-2234. Retro-futurism, Arthur thought. They liked to remind you who paid for the air. The meeting room was a small oval with a table of pale wood and a single window looking out onto the station’s spin ring. A woman waited there alone. She was perhaps fifty, Martian-born by the faint tan of her forearms, Earth-born by the cut of her suit. No insignia. No guards visible. She stood as he entered. “Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming. I am Consul Ilya Maren of Antares.” Arthur stopped a pace from the table. “You’re not diplomatic.” “No,” she said, and smiled without warmth. “We are practical. Please sit.” He sat. The air filtration drone was louder here. “You have a vein,” she said. “Azra. Grade four, possibly five. Under your lease on Plot 7-Gamma, Valles Marineris.” Arthur kept his hands flat on the table. “My surveyor’s report is filed with Helion Mining. It’s a modest strike.” “Modest strikes don’t bring three corporate security teams to your door in one night,” Maren said. “Nor do they bring the Martian Provisional Council to ask why you haven’t reported a strategic mineral.” “So I’m in the middle.” “You are exactly in the middle. Which is why we are here.” She slid a data-slate across the table. “Azra accelerates radioactive decay. You know that. What you may not know is why that matters now.” “I know it makes drives cheaper. And weapons faster.” “Correct. The Helion Consortium wants Azra for their jump-core program. The Terran Defense Pact wants it for their pulse warheads. The Free Martians want it to make Mars independent. Everyone wants it, Mr. Neegan, and everyone is willing to kill for it.” Arthur looked at the slate. A schematic of a drive coil glowed faintly. “And you?” “We want it not to be used at all, for a while,” Maren said. “Antares has been buying leases quietly for twenty years. We have a buffer zone around the most volatile veins. Yours is now in that zone.” “By buying me out?” “By offering you a choice. Option one: you sign over mineral rights to Antares at fair market value, plus a lifetime stipend and citizenship on Antares Prime. You go home, you live comfortably, and no one ever knows you found it.” “And option two?” She leaned forward. “You keep the lease. We register you as a protected scientific asset. You work for us, under contract, to study the vein. You tell Helion and the Council exactly what they want to hear. You do not sell. You do not drill. You let us control the narrative until we understand what Azra really does.” Arthur frowned. “That’s a lie.” “That is diplomacy,” she said. “The difference is we pay you to lie, and we protect you while you do it.” “Why me? I’m an engineer, not a spy.” “Because you are first generation,” Maren said. “You have no family on Earth to threaten, no debts to Helion. You built your hab with your own hands. People like you are rare, and therefore trustworthy. Also, you are already a problem. Problems are useful if they are managed.” The drone in the vents hit a slightly higher note. Arthur felt the familiar tightness in his chest that meant pressure change. “What happens if I say no?” he asked. “Then the Provisional Council will declare your plot a public hazard and seize it. Helion will file an injunction. The Defense Pact will send an inspector. You will be buried in paperwork and then in a suit. We are the only party offering you a way out with your life and your name intact.” She tapped the slate. “Azra is not just a metal, Mr. Neegan. It is a clock. It speeds up decay. Put enough of it near a reactor and you can make a star in a bottle. Put enough of it near a city and you can make a ghost town. The big picture is that humanity is about to learn how to move between stars and how to erase them. The small picture is that you have a hole in the ground on Mars that makes both possible.” Arthur stared at the window. The spin ring turned slowly, a ring of lights and lives. “Give me time,” he said. “You have until the shuttle returns to Mars,” Maren said. “After that, the other parties will have their own invitations for you. And they will not be polite.” She stood. The meeting was over. Arthur remained seated as the air filtration system hummed on, persistent and indifferent, as if it had been listening all along.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Asimov's classic sci-fi style while delivering the requested scenario. The author effectively establishes the retrofuturistic atmosphere through details like brass donor plaques and mechanical air filtration systems, creating that distinctive mid-20th century vision of the future that characterizes golden age science fiction. The dialogue-heavy structure works well, with Consul Maren serving as an effective exposition vehicle while maintaining natural conversational flow. Her character comes across as appropriately calculating and diplomatic, though Arthur feels somewhat passive throughout the exchange. The power dynamic is clear, but Arthur's responses could be more distinctive to his character as a first-generation settler and engineer. The world-building successfully operates on both macro and micro levels, as requested. The larger political machinations involving multiple factions (Helion Consortium, Terran Defense Pact, Free Martians, Antares) create a believable web of competing interests, while smaller details like the pressure changes and recycled air ground the reader in the immediate setting. The explanation of Azra's properties and implications feels organic to the conversation rather than forced exposition. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with effective sensory details like the "persistent mechanical drone" and "smell of recycled air and hot plastic." The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through the journey to the meeting and maintaining it through the negotiation. The ending appropriately leaves Arthur (and the reader) in suspense while establishing clear stakes. However, the piece suffers from some predictability in its setup and resolution. The "mysterious powerful organization offers protection in exchange for cooperation" scenario follows familiar patterns, and Arthur's ultimate position as a pawn is telegraphed early. The characterization, while competent, lacks the psychological depth that would elevate this from solid genre writing to memorable fiction. The technical execution is strong, with natural sentence flow and appropriate tone throughout. The piece successfully plants seeds for larger intrigue while maintaining focus on the immediate dramatic situation. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smells like vinegar and warm metal. Red light makes everything look like a bruise. I’m 25 and I’m supposed to be good at this. I’m the one who tells people where to stand, how to hold the light, when to stop fucking around and actually make art. My professor calls me assertive. My exes called me a lot of other things. I like the darkroom because it’s the only place where nobody can see me fidget. Elliot is already at the enlarger when I get in. He’s 19, he/him, and he wears thrift-store nu-goth like it was tailored for him — black corduroy pants, a vintage band tee with the sleeves cut off, silver rings on every finger. He’s been in my experimental photo class since September and I’ve been watching him like a creep. Not in a bad way. Just... quietly fascinated. He’s got this softness that doesn’t match the aesthetic. He listens. He asks questions about film grain like it’s a language he wants to learn properly. Tonight we’re paired for the final. Professor Chen wants a series on “self-portrait as other.” We’ve been working on a contact sheet of Elliot’s hands holding different objects — a dead moth, a chipped mug, my Polaroid camera. I took the photos. He’s been developing. “Hey,” he says, and doesn’t look up. His hair falls into his eyes. He’s got ink on his cheek from where he wiped it. “Hey,” I say, too loud. The red light makes my voice sound wrong. I drop my bag. My leather jacket clinks against the metal sink. We work in silence for a while. That’s the thing about darkrooms. You can’t talk too much because the timer is ticking and the chemicals are doing their thing. The safelight hums. My hands are in the developer and I can feel the cold through my gloves. Elliot pulls a print from the tray. It’s his hand around a cracked mirror. The image is too dark. “It’s not working,” he murmurs. I want to say *let me fix it*. That’s my instinct. Take charge. Adjust the exposure, tell him to hold still, make it better. Instead I say, “Show me what you want it to be.” He hesitates. Then he tells me. Not about the photo. About himself. “I’ve been thinking... about how I look,” he says. He’s staring at the print like it’s a shield. “Like, I like the clothes. I like being... I don’t know. Soft? But also... I don’t know if I want to be a boy all the time. Sometimes I want to try things and it feels scary because I don’t want people to think I’m...” He trails off. “I don’t know what I am yet. I just know I’m tired of pretending I’m sure.” The red light makes his face look younger. He’s 19 and he’s telling me this in a room the size of a closet, and I’m 25 and I’ve never wanted to be careful with anyone more in my life. My first thought is stupid and honest: *God, I’ve been crushing on you since October.* My second thought is worse: *What does that make me?* I’ve always been into defined things. Defined jawlines, defined roles. Guys who knew what they wanted and let me take the lead. Elliot is all questions. He’s quiet intellect and thrift-shop nu-goth and he’s questioning his gender in a red-lit room while his hands shake in developer. I don’t know what to do with my assertiveness. I want to protect him. I want to say *I’ve got you, it’s fine, you can be anything.* But that’s just me taking charge again, making his vulnerability about my ability to handle it. So I don’t. I just sit on the stool next to him and let the silence be there. “I like how you look,” I say, and it comes out too fast. “I mean — I like... you. The way you think about it. It’s... exciting.” He blinks. “Exciting?” “Yeah.” I’m aware of how much I’m exposing myself and I can’t stop. “I’ve never... I don’t know. I’m used to people who are sure. You’re... you’re figuring it out in real time and it’s kind of beautiful to watch.” He smiles a little, shy and embarrassed. “You’re not scared I’m gonna be confusing?” I laugh, because it’s awkward and I need the sound. “Babe, I’m a photography major. Confusing is my medium.” That makes him laugh too. It’s small, but it breaks something open. He tells me about wanting to try his sister’s eyeliner. About hating his name some days. About loving his hands. I tell him about the time I dyed my hair blue and my mom cried. We’re both in the red light and it feels like confession without the church part. Then the door to the darkroom opens. Just a crack. The hallway fluorescents spill in. I swear. Elliot yelps and slams his hand down on the stack of paper on the counter to cover it. Too late. The light hits the whole box. A whole box of 8x10 RC paper, the good stuff we pooled for, just... flashes white. “Oh my god,” he whispers. “Oh my god, Dani, I’m so sorry.” I stare at the paper. It’s ruined. Fogged. Useless. My brain does the math — we’re out of budget, we’re on a deadline, I’m the one who should have taped the door shut. “Hey,” I say, and my voice is softer than I’ve ever heard it. I reach over and put my hand over his on the ruined stack. “It’s just paper.” “It’s not just paper,” he says, panicking. “We needed that.” “I know.” I squeeze his fingers. They’re cold. “We’ll figure it out. We have the negatives. We’ll print smaller. Or we’ll ask Chen for more. It’s fine.” He looks at me like I’ve just told him the sky isn’t falling. He exhales and his shoulders drop. The red light catches the silver in his rings. “We’re out of time,” he says, but he’s not talking about the paper anymore. I know what he means. The timer dings. The print he was working on is done. He lifts it out, water dripping. It’s his hand holding the mirror, but this time he’s looking directly at the camera. Clear. Present. I want to take charge. I want to tell him what this means, what I feel. Instead I just nod at the print. “That’s good.” “Yeah,” he says. “It’s me.” We sit there in the bruised light, two people in uncharted territory, with a box of dead paper between us and a timer that’s still ticking. And for the first time in a long time, I don’t feel like I have to lead. I just feel like I’m here.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive 25-year-old art student while showing her vulnerability when confronted with Elliot's gender questioning. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both as literal backdrop and metaphorical space for revelation and intimacy. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and well-developed. Her attraction to Elliot is portrayed with complexity - she's drawn to his unconventional masculinity while simultaneously questioning what his gender exploration means for her own identity. Elliot emerges as more than just a plot device; his vulnerability feels genuine rather than performative. The prose style effectively balances literary sophistication with accessibility. Sentences like "Red light makes everything look like a bruise" and "The red light makes his face look younger" create atmospheric consistency without becoming overwrought. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, particularly Elliot's hesitant self-revelation and Dani's response. The narrative structure builds tension effectively through the intimate darkroom conversations, leading to the accidental paper exposure that serves as both literal crisis and metaphorical moment of clarity. The ending avoids false resolution while providing emotional satisfaction - both characters remain in "uncharted territory" but with deeper understanding. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the darkroom as confessional space, the red light symbolism, and the accidental exposure serving as catalyst. The piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining Dani's attraction and internal conflicts. Some dialogue exchanges, while realistic, lack the spark that would elevate them from good to exceptional. The emotional complexity is handled with maturity, avoiding both sensationalism and oversimplification of gender identity issues. The piece respects both characters' journeys without rushing toward easy answers or transformations. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
9:12 AM — Trevi Fountain The guidebook was open to *Fountains of Rome* and Ben was reading it like a prayer book, one foot in the Trevi, the other on the cobbles, when the Vespa screamed around the corner. Alessandra braked inches from his ankle. The bike shuddered, a blue Vespa PX with a bright yellow scratch across the rear panel where someone had once clipped it and she’d never bothered to repaint. She was helmet off, hair damp, a courier bag slung across her chest. “Ma che cazzo stai facendo?” she snapped, in Italian too fast for him. “Cammini come un nonno con la cataratta!” Ben flailed his hands. “I’m sorry! I’m so sorry! Scusi, scusi, I didn’t see you — I was —” She stared at the guidebook in his hands. “Trevi Fountain. Page 47. You’re going to throw a coin in, yes? Very romantic.” “It’s tradition,” he said, flushing. “I read—” “You read. You don’t live.” She swung a leg off the bike. Up close she was all sharp angles and heat, a faded *Roma* t-shirt under a leather jacket, eyes the color of espresso. “I’m Alessandra. And you’re about to be late for your sabbatical.” Ben offered a hand. “Ben. From Oxford. I’m on sabbatical. Studying—” “Love.” She grinned. “Everyone’s studying love here.” She didn’t wait for his answer. She flicked her wrist and the bike roared back to life. 11:03 AM — Via del Corso “Salta su,” she said. “I can’t— I don’t have a helmet—” “You’ll live.” She tossed him the spare, a pink one with a chipped visor. “Hold on.” He did. The city blurred. She weaved through traffic with a laugh that sounded like an insult. He clutched her waist, absurdly polite even mid-air. “Your bike is beautiful,” he shouted over the engine. “It has character,” she shouted back. “Like me.” At a red light she reached into her bag and produced two sugar packets from the bar they’d just passed. She slipped one into his jacket pocket. “For later.” He didn’t notice. 1:47 PM — Mercato di Testaccio She dragged him into the market without asking. Stalls of tomatoes, fish, men shouting prices. She bought him a paper cone of fried artichokes and then, while the vendor was distracted haggling with an old woman, her fingers brushed a sprig of rosemary from the bunch and tucked it behind his ear. “Che?” he said, bewildered, mouth full. “You smell like a trattoria now,” she said. “Better than guidebook.” A child ran past with a balloon. Alessandra caught it in one hand, popped it with her teeth, and let the rubber snap against Ben’s sleeve. He jumped, then laughed despite himself. “You’re terrifying,” he said. “Only on Tuesdays,” she said. She paid for the artichokes with coins she didn’t have enough of, then slipped a small brass keychain shaped like a Colosseum from the vendor’s tray into her palm as she handed over the money. The vendor never looked up. 4:20 PM — Trastevere Rooftop The building had no sign. She knew the super. The door was unlocked. They climbed six flights of stairs that smelled of laundry and garlic. On the roof, Rome opened up — terracotta and laundry lines and the dome of St. Peter’s far off. Ben sat on an overturned crate, knees to his chest. “I’ve never been on a roof in Rome,” he said quietly. “I was going to write about the Baroque.” “And now you’re writing about me,” she said. She was barefoot, picking at a loose tile at the edge. When he wasn’t looking she pried it up, pocketed the little ceramic fragment, and set the tile back down. “Do you always do this?” he asked. “Do what?” “Take people places they didn’t plan to go.” She shrugged. “You were planning to stay in the Trevi until the water ran out.” He laughed. It was a real laugh, unguarded. “You’re right.” She leaned closer, and for a second he thought she might kiss him. Instead she stole the guidebook from his lap, flipped to a blank page at the back, and wrote her number in looping script. Then she handed it back. “Don’t call,” she said. “Text. I don’t answer to professors.” 7:55 PM — Ponte Sisto The sun was bleeding over the Tiber. She’d dropped him at his pensione with a promise to bring him back. Now she was here, bike idling, the yellow scratch catching the last light. Ben stood on the bridge with his hands in his pockets, rosemary still behind his ear, sugar packet still in his jacket. He looked completely lost and completely happy. “You’re late,” he said. “You’re early,” she said. He hesitated, then said in careful Italian, “È stata una giornata… incredibile.” She smiled, sharp and soft at once. “You’re learning.” She swung off the bike. For a moment she just looked at him, as if deciding whether to keep him. Then she reached into her courier bag and pulled out a small, stolen ceramic tile, the one from the roof, and pressed it into his palm. “For your research,” she said. “A fragment of Rome. Don’t put it back.” He closed his fingers around it. “Alessandra—” “Don’t,” she said, already turning back to the bike. “You’ll ruin it with footnotes.” She kicked the Vespa to life. The engine snarled. She didn’t look back, but she waved once, a quick flick of her wrist, as if she might steal one more moment and then let it go. Ben stood on the bridge long after she was gone, the tile warm in his hand, the rosemary wilting behind his ear, utterly disoriented and, against all his scholarly intentions, utterly smitten.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative storytelling within the contemporary romance framework. The author successfully creates a vivid day-long journey through Rome using interconnected vignettes that reveal character through action and dialogue rather than exposition. The characterization is particularly effective. Alessandra emerges as a compelling figure whose kleptomania is woven naturally into the narrative through subtle actions - stealing sugar packets, rosemary, a keychain, and the ceramic tile. These moments feel organic rather than forced, revealing her mischievous nature without heavy-handed explanation. Ben's transformation from bumbling academic to willing participant feels earned through the progression of scenes, each pushing him slightly further from his comfort zone. The dialogue crackles with authenticity, capturing the cultural clash between Alessandra's rapid-fire Italian directness and Ben's overly polite British reserve. Lines like "You read. You don't live" and "You'll ruin it with footnotes" efficiently establish character while advancing the romantic tension. The mix of Italian phrases adds authenticity without becoming inaccessible. The prose style is economical yet evocative, using precise details to create atmosphere - the "blue Vespa PX with a bright yellow scratch," the market that "smells of laundry and garlic," the sun "bleeding over the Tiber." The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality through carefully chosen imagery. The structure works well, with timestamps creating a sense of real-time progression while each scene builds romantic and narrative tension. The pacing accelerates appropriately, mirroring Ben's increasing comfort with spontaneity. However, some elements feel slightly predictable within the genre conventions - the motorcycle tour, the rooftop scene, the parting gift. While executed well, these beats follow familiar romantic comedy patterns. The ending, though satisfying, doesn't surprise beyond genre expectations. The piece succeeds in creating genuine chemistry between the protagonists and establishes a strong foundation for a longer work, fulfilling the prompt's requirements effectively. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I wipe down the bar with a rag that’s seen better centuries and watch the Outpost breathe. The Last Outpost is a hollowed rock with good lighting and bad acoustics. Miners in soot-stained jumpsuits, merchants with too many rings, a couple of drift kids who pay in data. The air smells like recycled coffee, cheap synth-lime, and the faint ozone of the docking clamps cycling out there in the belt. “Your usual, Hark?” I ask. He lifts his prosthetic and taps it against the counter like it’s a glass. “Two fingers of that brown stuff you keep calling whiskey. And tell Lina her price on iridium is insulting.” Lina, who is three stools down and pretending not to listen, snorts. “Tell Hark his mine is a hole in the ground with delusions of grandeur.” “Delusions pay,” Hark says. “You pay in compliments.” I pour. “I pay in drinks. Same as always.” Mira slides a chit across the bar. “One Vega for the road. Neat. You’re not going to water it down just because you think I’m pretty.” “You’re pretty,” I say, and I mean it. “I’m not an animal.” She grins. “Good. I like animals.” The chime over the airlock door goes soft. It’s not the usual burst of boots and banter. It’s quiet. A single person steps in, shaking the dust of the belt off his coat. His dreads are tentacled, the kind that move on their own, and they’re askew, half-tangled around his shoulders like he’s been running. He’s pale under the bar lights, eyes too wide. He doesn’t look at anyone but me. He slides onto the stool at the far end, the one by the emergency exit. “Vega whisky, neat,” he says. “Better make that a double.” I don’t move right away. “You got credits?” “I got a name,” he says. That should be enough to make me pour. It isn’t. I set the bottle down. “Names don’t buy drinks here,” I say. “Credits do. Or a story. You look like you’re out of both.” He laughs, a thin sound. “You still talk like that, Nettle.” The rag stops in my hand. My name is Nets here. It’s been Nets for three years. “Don’t know a Nettle,” I say. My voice comes out steady. It’s a talent. He leans in. His dreads twitch. “You know me. You used to call me Rook. You used to pour me Vega when the Consortium wasn’t watching.” Hark frowns. “Who’s this?” “No one,” I say quickly. “Just a customer.” Rook — if that’s his name — doesn’t look away. “You’re good at that. Still keeping the peace.” “I keep the bar clean,” I say. “That’s my job.” He holds out his hand. It’s shaking. “I need a minute. Just a minute before they find me.” Lina watches us both in the mirror behind the bottles. “You know him?” “I know a lot of people,” I say. “Most of them I don’t serve.” “Please,” he says. “Double. Neat. I’ll pay.” I pour because pouring is what I do. The amber catches the light. He watches the stream like it’s water. “Thank you,” he says. A glass breaks somewhere in the background, a clean sharp crack off the far table where the drift kids are playing cards. One of them curses, someone laughs, it gets swept up in the noise. I don’t look. “You shouldn’t be here,” I say quietly. “The Outpost is neutral. You bring trouble, you bring it on everyone.” “I’m not bringing trouble,” he says. “I’m trying to leave it.” “You’re Rook,” I say. “You were trouble when you were clean-shaven.” He swallows. “I’m not here for you. I’m here for a package. It’s in the airlock. Small. I need you to hold it for me until my ship comes in.” My stomach does that old flip. “No.” “It’s not weapons,” he says. “It’s a data shard. Names. Accounts. Proof that the Consortium sold out the Belt workers last cycle. You always said you wanted to do something useful with your talents.” I think about the Outpost. About how they tolerated my flaws. About how I try to keep them in equilibrium with my assortment of talents. Lying is a talent. So is making people feel safe. So is knowing when to pour and when to pour out. “You’re asking me to hide contraband,” I say. “I’m asking you to be Nettle for five minutes,” he says. “Not Nets.” Mira touches my arm. “You okay? You’ve gone pale.” “I’m fine,” I say. “Just a long night.” Rook sets a credit chip on the bar. It’s black and unmarked. “Double,” he says again, like he hasn’t heard me. The airlock chime goes again. Louder this time. Two people. Boots. A voice over the comm crackles through the Outpost speakers, low and official. “Attention Outpost. We have a warrant for one Rook Varren, Cephalid, wanted for data theft and evasion. Do not grant passage. Repeat, do not grant passage.” Hark stands up. “Well, hell.” Lina is already sliding off her stool. “You know him?” I look at Rook. He looks at me. His dreads are still askew. “Please,” he says. “Just hold it.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece successfully establishes the cozy sci-fi atmosphere of The Last Outpost while introducing compelling conflict through Rook's arrival and the revelation of Nets' hidden past. The writing demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt requirements, maintaining first-person present tense throughout and achieving approximately the requested dialogue ratio. The characterization is particularly effective. Nets emerges as a complex protagonist whose bartending role serves as both literal occupation and metaphor for her peacekeeping nature. Her dialogue feels authentic and reveals character through subtext - her deflections, her careful word choices, and her protective instincts toward the Outpost community. The supporting cast, though briefly sketched, feels lived-in through natural banter between Hark and Lina. The world-building is efficiently handled through concrete details rather than exposition dumps. References to "recycled coffee," "synth-lime," "drift kids who pay in data," and "docking clamps cycling" create a believable future setting without overwhelming the narrative. The Outpost feels like a real place with its own social dynamics and unwritten rules. The conflict escalates naturally from personal tension to broader stakes. Rook's request to hide contraband forces Nets to choose between her carefully constructed new identity and her past principles. The arrival of authorities via comm announcement creates immediate external pressure while the data shard's contents (evidence of Consortium corruption) adds moral complexity. The prose style is clean and purposeful, avoiding purple prose while maintaining atmospheric detail. Dialogue feels natural and serves multiple functions - advancing plot, revealing character, and building tension. The pacing builds effectively toward the cliffhanger ending. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the mysterious stranger with a past connection to the protagonist is a familiar trope, though it's executed competently here. The writing occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in establishing Nets' reputation and talents. The ending appropriately leaves the central conflict unresolved while raising stakes through the warrant announcement. This creates genuine tension about Nets' choice and the potential consequences for the Outpost community. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
A street musician's saxophone plays in the background as I walk down a crowded street and I swear it sounds like it's crying on purpose. Or maybe that's just me. It's loud here. Too loud. Bourbon Street smells like beer and fryer oil and people. My shoes are already wet from last night's rain and the soles are coming apart. The backpack Mom packed for me — she thought I was going to a sleepover, she thought — is digging a bruise into my shoulder. I have $37, a dead phone, a library card with my dead name on it, and a hoodie that says TENNESSEE VOLS that I stole from my brother's closet because it was the only thing big enough to hide in. I walked here from where that guy dropped me. He said New Orleans was too far, too weird, he wasn't doing a kidnapping. He said it like I was a problem he solved. I didn't argue. I just got out before he changed his mind and called the cops. Two days ago I told them. I told Mom and Dad at the kitchen table after dinner. I practiced it for six months in the shower. *I'm trans. My name is Taylor.* Dad said nothing, just stared at his plate. Mom cried. Then Dad said, "We love you but we don't know you." The school counselor called the next morning and used the phrase "concerning behavioural patterns" like I was a file. Like I was a risk assessment. Now I'm in a city where nobody knows my dead name. That should feel like freedom. It mostly feels like free-fall. I duck under a string of fairy lights to get out of the sun. My throat is raw. I haven't eaten since the gas station in Mississippi where I bought a gas station coffee and the guy behind the counter looked at me like I was twelve. I'm sixteen. I look fourteen. That's a problem. "Hey, kid. You lost?" I turn. A girl is sitting on a milk crate outside a closed shop, picking at the paint on her nails. She's maybe seventeen, maybe nineteen, with bleached tips and a silver hoop through her eyebrow. A duffel bag is propped against her leg with a tag that says AIRBNB. Her sneakers are covered in mud. I shake my head. "Just passing through." She grins. "We all are." She gestures to the street with her chin. "You got a place to crash tonight or you gonna sleep under that saxophone guy?" The saxophone is still wailing. I don't answer. I am trying to do the math: if I sleep outside, I get robbed. If I talk to her, I get robbed. If I keep walking, I get lost. She stands up, stretches. "I'm Lila." She offers a hand. I look at it. My hand is shaking. I take it because it feels rude not to. Her palm is calloused. "Taylor." "Cool name." She doesn't ask what pronouns. I don't know if that's good or bad. "You run?" The question hits too fast. My stomach flips. "Yeah." She nods like she expected it. "Me too. Ran from Baton Rouge last month. My mom's boyfriend. You?" I want to say Tennessee. I want to say trans. I want to say my dad said he didn't know me. Instead I say, "Family stuff." She sits back down and pats the crate. "Family stuff is the best kind of stuff. Nobody believes you." I sit. The wood is warm from the sun. The saxophone keeps playing and a little girl runs past us with a balloon that says I LOVE NOLA. "You got money?" Lila asks, casual. I shake my head. She pulls a crumpled five from her pocket and slides it across. "For a po'boy. You look like you haven't eaten." I stare at it. "I can't take your money." "You can. And then you owe me a story." She taps her temple. "I collect them. Better than a phone charger." I take it. My fingers are numb. "Deal." We walk to a place with a line. She orders for me. I watch her talk to the guy behind the counter like she knows him. She does. Everyone knows everyone here, it seems. That's terrifying. We eat on the curb. The bread is soggy and the meat is good. I am crying a little and I tell myself it's the onion. "You're quiet," she says. "I'm tired." "You're scared." She says it without judgment. "You should be. First day is the worst. Second day you start making mistakes." I laugh, a short, broken sound. "I already made a mistake. I came here." "Nah." She wipes her hands on her jeans. "Mistake is trusting the wrong person. I haven't done that in a while." I look at her. She has a scar on her jaw I hadn't noticed. "You have issues," I say. It's stupid. She shrugs. "You don't?" I think about the counselor. About Mom's voice on the phone last night, crying, saying come home. About the way Dad didn't look at me. About the name I want to use and the name on my ID. About being sixteen and having to be a whole person before I even know how to be a kid. "I have secrets," I say. She smiles, small and real. "Good. Keep 'em. I got my own." She pulls a little silver locket from under her shirt. Inside is a photo of a boy with a gap tooth. She doesn't show me the rest. "You ever think about going back?" I ask. "Every day," she says. "Then I remember why I left." We sit in silence for a minute. The saxophone guy packs up. The street gets busier. Tourists with beads and sunburns. Lila stands. "Come on. I know a place we can sleep that's not a jail cell. It's not great, but it's dry." My brain screams no. My body is so tired it screams yes. "I don't know you," I say. "I know you," she says. "You're hungry and you're running and you think you have to do it alone. You don't." I stand up. My legs are shaky. The backpack feels lighter for a second. "Okay," I say. "But if you try to rob me, I'm kicking you." She laughs. "Deal." We walk down the crowded street together, and for the first time since I got dropped off, the saxophone in the background doesn't sound like it's crying. It just sounds like music.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Taylor's voice as a transgender teen runaway navigating their first day in New Orleans. The writing maintains consistent first-person perspective with mixed tense as requested, and incorporates both internal monologue and dialogue effectively. The characterization is nuanced and believable. Taylor's vulnerability, fear, and cautious hope feel authentic for a sixteen-year-old in crisis. The internal conflict between desperation and self-preservation drives realistic decision-making. Lila emerges as a compelling secondary character with her own implied backstory and street-smart pragmatism, avoiding the trap of being merely a plot device. The prose style is generally elegant and controlled, with strong sensory details that ground the reader in New Orleans' atmosphere. Lines like "A street musician's saxophone plays in the background as I walk down a crowded street and I swear it sounds like it's crying on purpose. Or maybe that's just me" establish both setting and emotional state efficiently. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, revealing character through subtext. Lila's casual "Family stuff is the best kind of stuff. Nobody believes you" conveys worldly experience while Taylor's hesitant responses show their inexperience with street life. The conversation flows organically without feeling forced or expository. Emotionally, the piece succeeds in creating complexity without melodrama. Taylor's conflicted feelings about their situation—the simultaneous relief and terror of being unknown—ring true. The ending strikes an appropriate balance, offering tentative hope without resolving Taylor's fundamental problems or erasing their trauma. However, some elements feel slightly predictable. The meeting with another runaway follows expected patterns, and while Lila is well-drawn, her role as experienced guide to Taylor's newcomer is somewhat familiar territory. The pacing occasionally slows during descriptive passages, though not severely. The piece demonstrates strong technical control and emotional intelligence, creating an engaging opening chapter that honors the complexity of its subject matter while maintaining readability. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Midas stared at Chewy and Chewy stared at the wall, which was the best Chewy could manage since the left eye had been eaten by moths in 2038 and the right eye now blinked on a three-second loop regardless of input. “Right,” said Midas. “We’re out of beans, the filter’s clogged with what I’m pretty sure is someone’s sock, and the rain barrel is full of frogs. So today we do something useful.” Chewy’s voice box, which had survived the Collapse, the Great Power Outage, and Midas’s attempt to rewire it with a paperclip, clicked on. “Wanna go get a snack?” it said cheerfully, in the tone of a mall mascot designed for children who had never seen a real koala. “We’re going to find the refuge,” Midas said. Chewy blinked. “Wanna go get a snack?” Yesterday, while scavenging the old bypass for copper wire, Midas had found a wall of the abandoned McMuffin Express that someone had taken very seriously. In charcoal, in neat block capitals, it read: > THE WATER TOWER LIES. THE REFUGE IS BELOW WHERE THE TREES GROW IN A CIRCLE. FOLLOW THE RED ARROWS. BRING NOTHING. Below it, in smaller, shakier letters: *ps. the bees are not the enemy.* Midas, who had a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble, interpreted this as a treasure map. Chewy, who had a knack for saying the same thing every four minutes, interpreted it as a suggestion. Home base was the service station on Route 9, where the pumps had long since become abstract sculpture and the forecourt was now a very respectable garden of dandelions and rust. Midas lived in the back office. Chewy lived on the counter next to the dead microwave, which Midas insisted was for company. “We’ll take the trolley,” Midas said, patting the shopping trolley he used for transport. It had one wheel, a shopping list from 2019 still in the basket, and a profound sense of destiny. Chewy blinked. “Wanna go get a snack?” The mission, as deliberated over cold tea and the remains of a granola bar, was simple: follow red arrows. Find refuge. Possibly get water. Possibly not die. It went sideways at the first arrow. The red arrows were painted on rocks, on fence posts, on the occasional bewildered badger. They led, with admirable consistency, into the woods that had reclaimed the old industrial park. The trees grew in a circle around a concrete slab, which was promising until Midas realized the slab was the top of a storm drain and the trees were growing in a circle because the drain was a perfect wind tunnel for seeds. “Brilliant,” Midas said. “Refuge below where the trees grow in a circle.” Chewy was perched on his head, because Chewy was heavy and Midas’s neck was weak. “Wanna go get a snack?” Midas lowered himself down the drain with a rope made of shoelaces and optimism. The rope held for approximately three seconds. The first sideways development was the discovery that the drain was not empty. It was full of water, very cold water, and a family of rats who had formed a small, well-organized government. The second sideways development was the discovery that the red arrows continued down the drain, painted on the walls by someone with a flashlight and a death wish. Midas followed them, slipping on algae, while Chewy bounced on his head and provided running commentary. “Wanna go get a snack?” At the bottom was a door. A real, metal, padlocked door with a sign: MUNICIPAL WATER STORAGE - AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY. Someone had spray-painted a red arrow pointing at it and the words *IT’S FINE*. Midas, who had a knack for trouble, tried the door. The padlock was rusted shut. He hit it with a rock. The rock bounced off. He hit it with Chewy. Chewy, being animatronic, did not appreciate this. His voice box shorted. “Wanna go get a—” *bzzt* “—snack?” The third sideways development was the bees. They were not the enemy. They were, in fact, very much the enemy, or at least the bees were the enemy of the man who had tried to open a municipal water storage door with a stuffed koala. They emerged from a hole in the ceiling with the quiet dignity of a landlord evicting tenants. Midas ran. He ran up the drain, slipped on the algae, and emerged into the circle of trees with a face full of stings and Chewy now stuck in his hair. The refuge, it turned out, was not below the trees. The refuge was the trees. Or rather, the refuge was the old water tower that the graffiti had said *lies*. The water tower was a hundred metres away, and it had been converted by a previous, saner generation of survivors into a very nice place to live. It had solar panels, a rain catchment system, and a sign on the door that said *NO TOURISTS*. Midas, covered in bee stings and drain water, knocked anyway. A woman opened the door with a crossbow. “We saw the arrows,” she said. “We put them there to keep people away from the drain. The bees are not the enemy. The drain is.” “Ah,” said Midas. “Right. Well, thanks for the tip.” He left. The return to home base was accomplished in multiple ways. First, Midas walked, limping, with Chewy dangling from his belt, because his head was now too sore for Chewy to sit on. Second, Midas was carried by a very confused deer who thought the shopping trolley was a predator and tried to help. Third, Midas crawled the last fifty metres because the deer had left him in the middle of the service station forecourt. Home base looked much the same. The frogs were still in the rain barrel. The beans were still gone. Midas set Chewy down on the counter. Chewy’s voice box had finally given up entirely and now just emitted a soft, mournful *bzzt*. Midas poured himself tea. He looked at the graffiti in his notebook and added a footnote: *Refuge exists. Do not go in drain. Bees are not the enemy, but drain is.* Chewy blinked. Once. Twice. “Tomorrow,” Midas said to no one in particular, “we’ll just stay here and get snacks.” Somewhere in the woods, a red arrow pointed faithfully toward a very wet, very ratty, very bee-adjacent municipal door, waiting for the next person with a knack for trouble and a stuffed koala for company.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, absurdist humor, and matter-of-fact treatment of bizarre situations. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both desolate and oddly cozy, populated by characters who approach survival with resigned pragmatism rather than heroic determination. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believable protagonist - not incompetent, but possessed of that particular brand of optimistic foolishness that leads to predictable disasters. His relationship with Chewy, the malfunctioning animatronic koala, provides both humor and pathos. Chewy's limited vocabulary ("Wanna go get a snack?") becomes a running gag that never overstays its welcome, while his gradual deterioration throughout the story adds subtle emotional weight. The prose style authentically echoes Pratchett's voice - the deadpan observations ("Chewy stared at the wall, which was the best Chewy could manage"), the footnote-style asides, and the way mundane details are treated with the same gravity as extraordinary ones. The author demonstrates particular skill in balancing humor with genuine stakes, never letting the comedy completely undermine the reality of their situation. The plot structure follows the prompt requirements effectively, moving from deliberation through inevitable failure back to home base. The mission's sideways progression feels organic rather than forced - each complication (the drain, the rats, the bees, the crossbow-wielding woman) emerges naturally from Midas's poor decision-making. However, the piece occasionally lacks the deeper philosophical undertones that distinguish Pratchett's best work. While the humor is consistent, it doesn't quite achieve the layered meaning that makes Pratchett's writing resonate beyond its immediate entertainment value. Some descriptions, while vivid, border on trying too hard for cleverness ("a rope made of shoelaces and optimism"). The ending strikes an appropriate note - neither triumphant nor devastatingly bleak, but realistically deflated. Midas learns something, but not too much, and the world remains fundamentally unchanged, which feels true to both the characters and the post-apocalyptic setting. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door of *Yr Athro* in Llanidloes jingled and then clanged again as the wind shoved it. Carys looked up from the returns. A man in a wet coat stood in the doorway with his hands in his pockets and his sunglasses still on, as if he thought that would help. “Closed for lunch,” she said, without looking up. “Come back at two.” He didn’t move. The rain was coming in behind him in a sheet. He took the sunglasses off. “Please,” he said. “Two photographers. One very persistent German. I’m not asking for anything dramatic. Just a minute.” Carys finally looked. He was taller than the doorframe suggested. Famous. She knew him from the telly, from the billboards on the A44. Finn Calloway. The rogue prince from *Blood & Lace*. The man who’d been photographed last month leaving a hotel in Cardiff with a woman who wasn’t his wife. He smiled. It was a practiced thing, the kind that made people lean in. “Finn Calloway,” he said, as if introducing himself to a fan. “You can tell me to sod off. I’ve had a lot of practice being told that today.” She put the book down. “I’m not telling you anything. I’m just not opening the door for them.” “Perfect.” He stepped in, shaking rain from his coat. “You’re a hero. I’m Theo. No, Finn. Sorry. The name’s Finn. I’m terrible with names when I’m nervous.” “You’re not nervous.” He laughed, a little too quickly. “I am. I’m very nervous. I’m a terrible liar. That’s why I do drama.” The bell jingled again as the door banged in the wind. Carys moved to close it. “If they see you in here, they’ll wait.” “They already are.” He gestured vaguely out the window. “They’ll wait till I’m dead or till you serve tea. Whichever comes first.” She didn’t smile. “We don’t serve tea.” “Oh.” He looked genuinely disappointed, then recovered. “Books then. I’ll buy a book. That’s a transaction. Very normal. Very Welsh. No one will notice a man buying a book.” “You’re loud.” “Am I?” He lowered his voice an octave. “I can be quiet. I’m very good at quiet. People say I’m very good at quiet.” Carys walked to the counter. “What do you want?” He scanned the shelves. “Something no one expects. Something with a spine. I’ve been on a set in Pinewood for six months playing a man who quotes poetry. I haven’t read anything since I was fourteen.” “Fourteen?” He shrugged, the charming rogue slipping for a half second. “My mum used to read to me. Then she stopped. Then I got an agent. Then I stopped reading. It felt… indulgent.” She handed him a battered paperback from the poetry section. *R.S. Thomas*. “That’s Welsh. You’ll hate it.” He took it like it was a gift. “I love being hated. It’s honest.” “You’re not here for honesty.” “No,” he admitted. “I’m here for a minute where nobody wants a photo. Where nobody claps.” She rang up the book. “That’s two pounds fifty.” He reached for his wallet, then stopped. “You don’t know who I am, do you?” “I know who you are.” “You don’t know me.” He said it lightly, but there was an edge under it. “Do you know that everyone likes me? It’s my job. It has to be. If one person doesn’t, the whole thing cracks.” Carys tapped the till. “I’m not going to like you.” He blinked. “Okay. Fair.” She was surprised at how quickly he recovered, how the smile slid back on. “You’re very pretty when you’re rude. Is that a Welsh thing?” “It’s a me thing.” He laughed again, but it was smaller this time. He turned the book over in his hands. “My dad told me once, after my first audition, ‘Don’t get used to it.’ He meant it kindly. He was a plumber. He thought fame was a leak. You patch it and it comes back. I’ve been trying to prove him wrong for twenty years. I’m terrified one day I’ll walk into a room and nobody will know me. Or worse, they’ll know me and not care.” The admission hung there. Carys didn’t soften. She just said, “That’s a fear.” “It’s the only one that makes sense.” She looked at him properly then. The rain had plastered his hair to his forehead. He was trying so hard to be liked it was almost painful. “You’re blocking the light,” she said. He stepped aside immediately, too quickly. “Sorry. Sorry. I’m very aware of my footprint.” She handed him the bag. “You can stay until the rain eases. Don’t talk to me.” He grinned, triumphant. “Deal.” He didn’t move to the poetry shelf. He sat on the floor by the window with his back to the glass, pretending to read. Every few minutes his eyes flicked up to her as she shelved returns, and she caught him watching the way she moved, the way she muttered under her breath at the dust. “You always talk to books?” he asked after a while. “I’m arguing with them. They never listen.” He snorted. “You’re immune. You know that? Most people fall apart when I do the thing.” “What thing?” “The charming thing. The ‘I’m a mess but I’m fun’ thing.” She didn’t answer. She shelved a novel and left a space where it didn’t belong. He leaned forward. “Why are you doing this? The cold shoulder. It’s a good look on you.” “Because you’ll leave faster if you’re not getting what you want,” she said. He studied her. The fragile ego was showing through the charm now, a thin skin underneath. “What do you want?” She almost laughed. “To finish my lunch.” He stood up, coat damp again. The rain had eased to a drizzle. “I should go.” “Probably.” He held the bag out. “Can I come back? When it’s not raining. When you’re not busy.” Carys looked at the door, then at him. “We’re closed Tuesdays.” “I’ll remember.” He didn’t kiss her hand. He didn’t try to get her number. He just nodded, as if she’d given him something real, and stepped back into the grey light. The bell jingled. He didn’t look back. She waited until the footsteps faded before she picked up the R.S. Thomas he’d left on the counter. He hadn’t opened it. She opened it for him.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Finn's performative charm masking insecurity, and Carys's dry, resistant Welsh pragmatism. The dialogue feels natural and carries the emotional weight effectively, with subtext running beneath surface interactions. The Welsh setting is well-integrated through specific details (Llanidloes, A44, R.S. Thomas poetry) without feeling forced. The bookstore *Yr Athro* provides an intimate, contained space that serves the story's needs perfectly. The author handles the "famous person hiding from paparazzi" premise with restraint, avoiding melodrama. Character development is particularly strong. Finn's fragile ego beneath the charm offensive is revealed gradually through dialogue and action rather than exposition. His admission about his father and fear of irrelevance feels earned. Carys's immunity to his charm, while being secretly affected, creates the requested dynamic convincingly. Her final gesture with the book provides subtle emotional resonance. The prose is clean and economical, with effective use of physical details (rain, the jingling bell, his wet hair) to ground the scene. The pacing builds naturally from initial resistance through gradual revelation to a satisfying conclusion that promises future possibility without forcing resolution. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where Finn's dialogue edges toward being overly articulate for someone genuinely flustered, and the R.S. Thomas reference, while authentic, might feel slightly precious. The ending, while well-executed, follows a somewhat predictable trajectory for this type of meet-cute scenario. The emotional complexity requested is present - both characters have clear internal conflicts that drive their external behavior. The chemistry builds believably through resistance and gradual revelation rather than instant attraction. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave under Aya’s palm with a sigh of old iron, not a shriek. That was the first wrong thing. She had expected tumblers, a ward, the thin chime of the scythan lock. The underhold of Morska House breathed out cold air that smelled of brine, damp brick, and the oil that never quite burned clean. The lamps along the vaulted throat were lit, low and steady, throwing amber halos onto wet stone. Too many lamps. Too still. Katra’s gloved fingers tightened on the hilt of her stiletto. Simeon pressed his back to the arch, his coat slick with sweat despite the chill. The three of them had come down the service stair with the practiced quiet of thieves, masks pulled low, boots silent on the iron grating. Now the quiet answered them. “Aya,” Simeon whispered. “It’s empty.” It was not empty. At the far end of the chamber, where the scythan reliquary sat on its dais beneath a lattice of cold iron and a sigil that pulsed faintly blue, a woman stood with her hands behind her back. Two bodyguards flanked her, broad men in oil-stained greatcoats, brass knuckles catching the lamplight, rifles cradled like offerings. The third man held a lantern up, and in its light Aya saw the guildmistress’s face. Eliza Morne. The Black Keel. Arrested six hours ago in the raid on the Salt Wharf. Aya had read the broadsheet that morning over tea in her father’s study, the ink still fresh: *MORNE TAKEN. GUILD LEADER IN CUSTODY.* She had laughed into her cup. The woman was unmanacled. Her hair, iron-grey and pulled back hard, was damp at the temples. A thin cut ran across her left cheek, already scabbing. She wore the same high-collared coat she’d worn in the portrait in the guild hall, the one with the brass buttons shaped like scythes. Aya’s throat went dry. *Mother,* she thought, absurdly, *you warned me about men who trust brass and oil and steel.* The immateria had never lied to her. It had whispered when she was twelve and the magistrates came for her mother, when the rope had creaked in the square. Magicka was feared and barely understood, and the men who feared it most were the ones who polished their rifles. “Well,” Morne said, her voice low and amused and utterly without surprise. “Well, well. The little aristocrat comes to play.” Katra stepped forward. “You’re supposed to be in the Black Cells.” “I was,” Morne said. “They gave me a cell with a window. The constable who took me likes to drink. He likes to talk. He liked my purse.” She inclined her head toward the bodyguards. “Boys, you know the drill.” Aya felt the pressure of hands before she saw them. One of the men took Katra by the elbow, firm, not cruel. Another took Simeon by the shoulder and turned him gently but completely around, the way one handles a skittish animal. The third moved to Aya. She did not resist. The mask was already slipping. “Don’t,” she said, too quickly. “Please.” The man’s fingers were cold. He lifted the edge of her domino with a thumb. The black silk came away, and the lamplight found her face — pale, unlined, the high cheekbones and the little mole beneath her left eye that the house portraits always caught. The face of Lady Aya Varnholt of the East Quarter, third daughter, noted in the society pages for her charitable work at the Orphanage of St. Brine. Simeon made a choked sound. Katra stared at the floor. Morne took a slow step forward. She did not smile. “You,” she said. “You are the ghost I’ve been hearing about in the lower wards. The girl who pulls knives from the air. The one who made Joss bleed without touching him.” Aya’s pulse hammered against her ribs. The immateria coiled low in her belly, a cold, curious thing. She could feel it listening. “I didn’t—” “You rose fast,” Morne said. “Too fast for a new knife. I thought it was a trick. A patron. Now I see it’s a birthright.” She looked at the sigil on the dais, then back at Aya. “Your mother was hanged for this. For pulling things from the dark. And you come down here to steal my heart.” A distant foghorn sounded from the harbor beyond the guild walls. Low, mournful, then a pause. A second. A third. The sound rolled through the stone and seemed to settle in Aya’s chest. “Please,” Aya said, and the word scraped. “You don’t want to kill me. Not here. Not like this.” Morne raised an eyebrow. “Why not?” “Because I’m worth more alive.” Aya forced her voice steady, the voice she used at dinner when her father spoke of tariffs. “You know my name now. You can’t unknow it. If you kill me here, my father will burn this house to the ground. He has the magistrates in his pocket. He has the Admiralty. He will call it a vendetta and the Crown will back him.” “Your father doesn’t know you’re here,” Simeon said, too loudly. “He will when you tell him,” Aya snapped, then softened. “He will when the body is found. And he will know it was you.” Katra found her voice, rough. “She’s got a point, Widow. The girl’s a leash. Pull it and the whole aristocracy comes down on you.” Morne studied her. The lamplight caught the scar on her cheek and the deep lines at the corners of her eyes. She was not a monster. She was a woman who had survived by knowing when to cut. “You think I care about your father’s purse?” Morne asked. “I think you care about the guild,” Aya said. “You just lost your leader in public. You need a story. You need a hostage who can open doors that steel can’t.” She swallowed. “I can get you the East Quarter charter. I can get you the dock permits my uncle’s been sitting on. I can get you men who trust brass and oil and steel because they think I’m one of them.” The immateria pulsed once, faintly, as if offended by the lie. Morne was silent for a long breath. The lamps hissed. “Unmask the boy,” she told her guard. Simeon’s mask came off. He was younger than Aya had realized, his eyes wide and wet. “And the girl,” Morne said. Katra did not move until the hand was on her face. The domino fell. Her hair was cropped short, her jaw set. Morne looked at the three of them, bound now in place by rifles rather than rope. “You’re clever, Lady Varnholt,” she said at last. “Your mother was clever too. It didn’t save her.” Aya’s stomach turned to water. She thought of the rope, the square, the way the crowd had gone quiet. She thought of the immateria, the dark entities she could summon with a thought, the way they whispered her name. “Then don’t hang me,” she said. “Use me. I’m a better investment than a corpse.” The foghorn’s third note faded into the brick. Morne smiled, thin as a blade. “Perhaps,” she said. “But first, I want to know what you were planning to do with my scythe.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric worldbuilding within the whalepunk fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a Victorian-gothic atmosphere through careful attention to sensory details - the "sigh of old iron," "brine, damp brick, and oil that never quite burned clean," and the interplay of lamplight and shadow. The prose maintains an appropriately gritty, period-appropriate tone throughout. The dialogue feels authentic to the setting and characters, with Morne's measured, threatening speech patterns contrasting effectively with Aya's desperate attempts at negotiation. The author handles the power dynamics well, showing Aya's quick thinking under pressure while maintaining the genuine threat posed by Morne and her guards. Character motivations are generally believable, particularly Aya's attempt to leverage her aristocratic status as a survival mechanism. The revelation of her identity creates appropriate tension, and her internal conflict about her magical heritage versus her social position adds depth. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension through the unexpectedly quiet entrance to the climactic unmasking and negotiation. The author successfully avoids writing a fight scene as requested, instead focusing on psychological tension and verbal sparring. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "too quiet" entrance immediately telegraphs a trap, and Morne's survival of arrest follows familiar patterns. The magical system (immateria) is mentioned but not deeply explored, leaving some worldbuilding elements underdeveloped. The prose occasionally veers toward overwrought territory with phrases like "the immateria coiled low in her belly, a cold, curious thing," though it generally maintains restraint. The ending feels appropriately dark and unresolved, fitting the gothic tone without false optimism. The piece successfully incorporates all requested story beats while maintaining narrative coherence and character consistency. The internal monologue effectively reveals Aya's psychological state without becoming intrusive.
