+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Court convened at the hour it always did, which was never quite. Dream sat. He was always sitting. The throne was a chair, a bed, a stone, depending on who was looking, and today it looked vaguely annoyed. A scribe made of moths took notes in a language that would forget itself by morning. The vaulted ceiling breathed. “Case 7-3-9,” the scribe said. “The Estate of Max, minor, recurring dreamscape, wildflower field.” First Love stood first. He was rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful, and wore a waistcoat that smelled faintly of first rain. He clutched a sheaf of petals like evidence. “My Lord,” he said, and blushed. “The dream was mine. Crafted. Curated. Seven months, every Thursday night, 22:14 to 22:47. The boy lies in the field. The girl — his crush, from Chemistry — sits beside him. There is a muddled almost-kiss. Pleasant confusion of emotions. Formative. Necessary.” Dream did not blink. He rarely did. Mora was already on the floor. She was not standing so much as settling. A heavy, damp weight. She smelled of cold kitchens and old linen. When she smiled, the air went thin. “Objection,” First Love said, too loudly. “She is *on* the witness stand.” “She’s on everything,” Mora said, and gave a faint cackle that echoed uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings. “Relax, little cupid. A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” Dream sighed. It sounded like a pillow being punched. “Proceed.” Mora spread her hands. The scribe’s moths shivered. “The boy’s breath is delicious,” she said, matter-of-fact. “Sweet, terrified, fourteen. First Love makes him lie down in a field and wait to be kissed by a girl who never quite commits. That is a perfect feeding posture. I merely improved the user experience. When she mounts him — playfully, as you say — she transforms. She is still attractive, confusingly so. Then she sits. On his chest. And feeds. He wakes up paralyzed, terrified, and *remembering her face*.” First Love turned an alarming shade of pink. “That is not romantic! That is assault!” “It is both,” Mora said. “Isn’t it? He thinks about her all day at school. He dreams about her all night. My involvement increased retention by sixty-three percent. I have the metrics.” Dream tapped a fingernail against his throne. The sound was wrong. “You subverted a registered formative dreamscape,” First Love said, his voice cracking. “You corrupted the narrative arc! The almost-kiss is sacred!” “The almost-kiss is inefficient,” Mora said. She cackled again, softer. “He never gets the kiss. He gets the *almost*. That’s hunger. I’m just the tax collector.” A long silence. Dream looked at the ceiling, then at First Love, then at Mora. The irritation was subtle, a tightening around his eyes that most entities mistook for eternity. “First Love,” Dream said at last. “You filed the dream under ‘First Love, minor.’ You did not file a restraining order.” “I — I assumed —” “You assumed the boy’s affection would remain pure,” Dream said. “It never does.” Mora leaned forward. The floor sagged. “My Lord, I ask only for continued access. Thursdays are good. He’s regular.” First Love clutched his petals. “He’s *fourteen*! He will develop a phobia of girls!” “He already has,” Mora said kindly. “It’s called puberty.” Dream stood. The courtroom rearranged itself to accommodate him, which was mostly inconvenience. “The dreamscape is contested,” he said. “The boy is the owner, though he does not know it. You are both tenants.” First Love brightened. Mora did not. Dream continued. “Therefore, the field of wildflowers remains. The girl remains. The almost-kiss remains.” First Love exhaled. “The chest-sitting remains,” Dream said. “On the condition that the transformation is mutual. When she mounts him, she will become terrifying and attractive. She will sit. She will feed. And she will *also* attempt the kiss while sitting.” Mora’s cackle rolled through the vault. It was delighted. First Love made a small, strangled noise. “My Lord, that is — that is grotesque.” “It is efficient,” Dream said. “You wanted formative experience. He will learn about breath, pressure, consent, terror, and confusing attraction all in one session. You wanted sustenance, Mora. You shall have it. With added emotional complexity.” Mora bowed her head, which was a lot of weight moving at once. “A fair compromise.” “One more thing,” Dream said, and the mischief was finally visible, a thin smile at the corner of his mouth. “The dream will now occur every night, not Thursdays. And the girl will remember it in waking life. Slightly.” First Love stared. “He’ll be afraid to talk to her.” “He’ll be unable to stop thinking about her,” Dream said. “Which was your goal.” The scribe’s moths finished writing and promptly forgot what they’d written. Mora settled back down, content. First Love left the courtroom clutching his petals, blushing harder than before. Dream watched them go, and for a moment the throne looked like a bed again. “Next case,” he said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully creating a dark fantasy courtroom scene with comedic elements set in Neil Gaiman's Dreaming universe. The author captures Dream's characteristic voice and demeanor effectively, portraying his irritation at having to adjudicate such petty matters while maintaining his otherworldly gravitas. The characterizations are well-executed and nuanced. First Love is portrayed as earnest but naive, clutching petals like evidence and blushing throughout. Mora is delightfully pragmatic and unapologetic, with her matter-of-fact delivery of disturbing content creating effective dark humor. Dream's growing irritation and eventual mischievous resolution feels authentic to the character. The prose style is appropriately spare and evocative, following the instruction to use descriptives sparingly. Lines like "The throne was a chair, a bed, a stone, depending on who was looking, and today it looked vaguely annoyed" and "A scribe made of moths took notes in a language that would forget itself by morning" create vivid imagery without overindulgence. The dialogue is particularly strong, with each character having a distinct voice. Mora's "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" and "It is both. Isn't it?" capture her pragmatic amorality perfectly. The courtroom procedural elements blend seamlessly with the fantastical setting. The resolution is clever and appropriately mischievous for Dream, forcing both parties to coexist in an increasingly complex arrangement that serves both their purposes while creating new complications. This feels earned rather than arbitrary. The dark humor is well-calibrated throughout, never becoming too light or too heavy. The piece maintains engagement through its brisk pacing and witty exchanges. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose could flow more naturally, and a few instances where the humor could be more subtle. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A crimson harvest moon casts ominous shadows on the deserted village streets. The air smells of cold stone, wet thatch, and iron. Somewhere a dog whimpers and stops. Yennefer of Vengerberg steps from the alley between the mill and the chapel, boots silent on the cobbles. The moon catches the violet of her eyes and the pale gold of her hair. Lilac and gooseberries cling to her skin even here, absurdly sweet against the rot. She does not hurry. She does not flinch. She feels him before she sees him. A wrongness settles in the throat of the street, a pressure that makes the hairs on her arms rise. Magic, but not the kind she knows. Old. Hungry. It tastes of blood and centuries. Alucard leans against a doorway, red coat hanging heavy with night, wide-brimmed hat tipped low, orange lenses catching the blood moon and throwing it back. He watches her with the bored amusement of a cat. In his gloved hands he holds two massive handguns, silver catching the light. He does not lower them. “You smell like a garden,” he says, voice smooth, amused. “In a graveyard.” Yennefer tilts her head. “And you smell like a crypt that learned how to wear a coat.” He smiles behind the lenses. “Flattering.” She has been tracking a plague of disappearances for three nights. Villagers vanish after dusk, throats torn, blood drained clean. The local priest called it a curse. The local witch called it a vampire. Yennefer called it an inconvenience. Now she finds the inconvenience standing in the street, immaculate, unhurried, and utterly at ease. “You are not from here,” she says. “I am from everywhere,” Alucard replies. “Tonight, I am from here. You?” “I am passing through.” The lie is thin and she does not bother to thicken it. He would see through it anyway. He sees everything. He pushes off the wall. The coat falls open, revealing a chest of pale, unnatural stillness. “You are a sorceress. I can taste the aether on you. It is... interesting. Most mages scream when they see me. You merely comment on my cologne.” Yennefer lifts a hand. The air shivers. A thin ribbon of violet fire curls between her fingers, then dies. “Most vampires scream when they see me. You merely comment on my perfume.” Power ticks between them, a taut wire. He is ancient, immense, a predator who has fed on armies. She is centuries old herself, reshaped by her own will, a woman who traded her spine for power and never apologized for the price. Neither blinks first. Alucard circles her slowly, boots clicking. “You altered yourself. Clever. Ugly is a weakness. You removed it.” Yennefer’s jaw tightens. “And you adorn yourself. Red coat, ridiculous hat, sunglasses at night. Vanity is a weakness. You embrace it.” He laughs, a low sound like breaking glass. “Weakness is a choice. I despise vampires who cannot accept their nature. They whine, they hide. I do not hide.” “You feed,” she says flatly. “You toy. You take pleasure in it.” “I take pleasure in worthy opponents,” he corrects. “The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame. Do you understand?” She does. She understands monsters who want to be killed. She has met them before. She does not step back. “Do you want me to kill you?” she asks. “I want you to try,” he says. “Your magic is pretty. It smells of lilac. I wonder if it tastes the same.” Repulsion rises in her, sharp and cold. The thing before her is not a man, not even a creature in the way she understands. It is a wound that learned to walk. And fascination rises with it, equal and unwelcome. She has studied forbidden texts, has walked the edge of infertility and power and loss. She knows what it is to be remade. He is remade by hunger. She flicks her wrist. The street erupts. A wall of force slams outward, shattering shutters, lifting dust. Alucard does not move. The force hits him and passes through, or he lets it pass, or he simply is not there. He is there. He grins. “Petty,” he says. She is not petty. She is precise. She draws a second circle of sigils in the air with her finger, and the moonlight bends. The blood moon flares, and for a heartbeat the shadows deepen, as if the night itself inhales. Alucard’s smile falters, just a fraction. Interesting. He raises one pistol. The silver bullet sings. Yennefer is already gone, a blur of motion and will, reappearing on the roof of the chapel. The bullet punches through the wood where she stood, splinters flying. “You are fast,” he says, and there is genuine appreciation in it. “For a mortal.” “I’m not sweet and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving,” she snaps, and hurls a bolt of raw chaos at him. He catches it in his bare hand. The energy crackles, blackens his glove, and then fades. He looks at his palm. No burn. He looks at her. “You are strong,” he admits. “Strong enough to be... inconvenient.” She lands in front of him, boots hitting cobble. The air between them hums. She could kill him. She knows the words, the old rites, the names that bind blood. He could unmake her in a heartbeat, tear her throat, drink her dry, and laugh while she begged. Neither moves to strike first. He lowers the pistols, just an inch. A concession, or a test. She lets the violet fire die in her palm. A concession, or a test. The blood moon watches. The village remains silent. “You will leave,” she says. “You will leave,” he says at the same time. They stare. The power dynamic shifts again, a pendulum that never finds center. He is monstrous and she is repulsed. She is powerful and he is fascinated. He wants a worthy end. She wants to be left alone. Finally, Alucard tips his hat. “Until next time, sorceress.” Yennefer turns, lilac and gooseberries trailing behind her like a warning. “Don’t follow me.” He does not. He watches her disappear into the dark, red coat a smear against the night, and he smiles. The moon keeps bleeding.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding. The author successfully captures both Alucard and Yennefer's distinctive voices and mannerisms, staying true to their source material while creating an original encounter. The medieval European setting is well-established through atmospheric details like cobblestones, chapels, and thatched roofs. The dialogue crackles with tension and wit, particularly in exchanges like Yennefer's "crypt that learned how to wear a coat" retort. Both characters maintain their established personalities - Alucard's sadistic amusement and desire for worthy opponents, Yennefer's sharp tongue and refusal to be intimidated. The power dynamic shifts are well-executed, with neither character gaining clear dominance. The prose strikes an effective balance between atmospheric description and action. Phrases like "wrongness settles in the throat of the street" and "a wound that learned to walk" are evocative without becoming overwrought. The blood moon imagery provides strong thematic cohesion throughout. The story structure works well for the length constraint, building tension through their verbal sparring before escalating to magical/physical confrontation, then pulling back to an uneasy standoff. This feels true to both characters - neither would easily submit or retreat. However, some elements feel slightly predictable. The "powerful beings circling each other" dynamic, while well-executed, follows expected patterns. The ending, though appropriate, doesn't offer significant surprises. Some descriptions occasionally veer toward purple prose, particularly in the opening paragraphs. The piece succeeds in creating a compelling encounter that feels authentic to both franchises while maintaining narrative tension throughout. The characterization is the strongest element, with both figures remaining true to their established personalities while revealing new facets through their interaction. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. The concrete is damp and cold, and the air smells like rust and old incense. The facility is not on any map. The walls breathe. Cells hold things that should not be held. Jolyne Cujoh is in Cell Block D. Her hair is in two buns, her orange prison jumpsuit is too big at the shoulders, and the butterfly tattoo on her left forearm catches the flicker. She is supposed to be doing push-ups. She is not. She hears soft footsteps. Makima stops in front of her cell. She is young, auburn hair tied neatly, ringed yellow eyes calm. She wears a white uniform that is too clean for this place. A leash hangs from her belt, empty for now. “Hello,” Makima says, voice sweet and even. “You must be Jolyne Cujoh.” Jolyne narrows her eyes. “Who the hell are you?” “I’m a visitor,” Makima says. “I’m here to see the interesting inmates.” Jolyne laughs, sharp and short. “Interesting? Bitch, I’m in here because some rich asshole framed me for murder. You look like a guidance counselor. You lost?” Makima smiles. It does not reach her eyes. “No. I’m exactly where I need to be. Your Stand is beautiful, you know. Stone Free. I’ve never seen someone unravel like thread.” Jolyne’s fingers twitch. Stone Free hums just under her skin. “You know about Stands?” “I know about a lot of things,” Makima says. “I know you can turn your body into string and make clothes and weapons and knots. I know you’re hot-headed and loyal and you don’t take disrespect. It’s very… human.” Jolyne stands up. “Don’t psychoanalyze me, freak. You got a name or you just gonna stand there smiling like a creepy doll?” “Makima,” she says. “And I’m not smiling at you. I’m smiling because I’m happy to meet you.” The light flickers. Jolyne watches Makima’s face for a twitch, a tell. There is none. “Happy my ass,” Jolyne mutters. “You’re too nice. Nobody’s this nice in a place like this.” “Is it nice to be nice?” Makima tilts her head. “I think it’s natural to be kind to people who are suffering.” Jolyne snorts. “Suffering? You’re the one with the leash. You keeping pets?” Makima’s smile thins, just a fraction. “I keep people safe.” Jolyne presses her palm to the cell bars. Stone Free begins to unravel from her fingertips, thin red string sliding out, testing the metal. “You’re not a guard. Guards don’t know what a Stand is.” “I’m not a guard,” Makima agrees pleasantly. “I’m the Control Devil. I make contracts. I make sure everyone gets what they want.” Jolyne’s string snaps back. “Devil? Like actual devil? Great, the prison’s got a devil on staff. That explains a lot.” “It explains why you’re still alive,” Makima says softly. “The facility likes to test things. You have power. I am intrigued by power that is not mine.” Jolyne’s jaw tightens. “You’re intrigued? That’s creepy.” “Is it?” Makima steps closer to the bars, close enough that Jolyne can see the faint reflection in her yellow eyes. “You’re suspicious of me. You think my demeanor is false. You’re right to be cautious. Suspicion keeps you alive.” Jolyne’s voice goes low. “You read me like a book.” “I read everyone,” Makima says. “It’s my job. Would you like a contract? You’re in a very difficult position. You could be free. You could have protection. All you have to do is… trust me.” Jolyne laughs, foul and loud. “If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney! I don’t do contracts with pretty girls who want to leash me.” Makima does not flinch. “You don’t have to trust me. You just have to listen.” The light flickers again, longer this time. In the dark, Jolyne hears a soft whimper from the cell down the hall. A dog, or something like a dog, paces behind its door. Makima follows her gaze. “He misses his owner. It’s sad, isn’t it? Dogs are supposed to die for their owners.” Jolyne’s stomach turns. “You’re sick.” “I’m practical,” Makima corrects. “You have friends outside, don’t you? Ermes, Weather Report, Emporio. They worry. I can make them safe. I can make you safe. In exchange for a little… cooperation.” Jolyne unravels more string, wrapping it around her wrist in tight coils. Stone Free can turn into a guitar string, a whip, a net. She can turn her whole body into it. She can get out. “You think I’m gonna bow down to you because you’re sweet?” Jolyne says. “I’ve been in prison for a year. I’ve fought Stand users, I’ve fought the system. You’re just another manipulator.” Makima’s expression stays gentle. “Manipulation is a strong word. I prefer guidance.” “Guidance my ass,” Jolyne snaps. “You want my Stand. You want to control it.” “I want to understand it,” Makima says. “Stone Free can unravel a person. Imagine what it could do with a devil. Imagine what it could do with me.” The corridor goes quiet. The flickering light steadies for a second, then stutters. Jolyne realizes Makima is not here to help her. She is here to collect her. The sweet tone, the soft questions, the offer of safety — it’s all bait. Makima studies her the way a handler studies a new dog. “You’re not a visitor,” Jolyne says slowly. “You’re the warden.” Makima smiles wider. “I’m whatever I need to be.” Jolyne’s string snaps taut against the bars. She can feel the power humming. She is impulsive, she is angry, she is not going to wait. “Get out of my face,” she growls. Makima tilts her head, still smiling. “You’re angry because you see the truth. That’s good. Angry people are honest.” Jolyne lunges. Stone Free erupts from her body in a spray of red thread, lashing toward Makima’s throat. The string moves faster than sight. Makima does not move. The string stops an inch from her skin, as if it hits invisible glass. “You can’t control me,” Makima whispers, and her voice is no longer soft. It is calm, absolute. “I decide who is beneath me.” Jolyne feels a pressure behind her eyes, a cold tug at her will. Her string slackens. Her knees want to buckle. She clenches her teeth and forces Stone Free to recoil, pulling the string back into her skin with a painful snap. She staggers back against the wall. Makima’s smile returns, pleasant and false. “See? We can talk like civilized people.” Jolyne breathes hard, her butterfly tattoo pulsing. She is not cool under pressure, she is burning. She hates how easily Makima mimics kindness. She hates how much she wants to believe it. “You’re a fucking nightmare,” Jolyne spits. “I’m a devil,” Makima says sweetly. “And you’re very interesting. I’ll be back.” She turns and walks away, footsteps soft on the concrete. The light flickers irregularly behind her. Jolyne watches her go, string coiled tight around her fists, and knows the battle has only just started.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt, successfully capturing both characters' essential traits and creating a tense supernatural prison encounter. The author effectively establishes Jolyne's hot-headed, suspicious nature and Makima's manipulative sweetness masking sinister control. The characterization is particularly strong. Jolyne's dialogue feels authentic - her profanity, defiance, and quick temper all ring true to the source material. The inclusion of her iconic Disney quote feels natural rather than forced. Makima's false pleasantness gradually revealing her true nature is well-executed, with subtle shifts in her dialogue that maintain her soft-spoken demeanor while revealing increasing menace. The atmospheric writing creates an effectively unsettling mood. The flickering lights, breathing walls, and mysterious sounds establish the supernatural prison setting without over-explanation. The prose maintains a consistent third-person present tense throughout, with a tone that balances Jolyne's raw energy against Makima's calculated calm. The dialogue carries the story effectively, revealing character motivations and escalating tension naturally. Each character's voice remains distinct - Jolyne's crude directness contrasts sharply with Makima's polite manipulation. The power dynamic shift when Makima demonstrates her control ability creates genuine tension. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The ending feels somewhat abrupt, though this may be intentional given the word limit. Some descriptions border on purple prose ("Stone Free erupts from her body in a spray of red thread"), though they generally serve the dramatic tension. The battle of wits, while present, could have been more intricate - it relies heavily on Jolyne's instinctive suspicion rather than complex psychological maneuvering. The imagery effectively uses both characters' signature elements - Jolyne's string abilities and Makima's leash symbolism. The supernatural prison setting provides an appropriate neutral ground for their confrontation. The pacing builds steadily from initial suspicion to direct confrontation, maintaining reader engagement throughout. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 72.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-8142 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** SCP-8142 is not a physical object. Containment consists of monitoring and documentation of the anomalous memo generation affecting Dr. Mara Kessler, Site-19 Researcher, Level 3 clearance. Dr. Kessler is to be housed in a standard private quarters with 24-hour visual monitoring. All Foundation memo paper stock in her assigned office and residence is to be inventoried weekly and secured under lock when not in active use. No memo paper is to be left unsecured in areas accessible to Dr. Kessler. Psychological evaluation is to be conducted bi-weekly by a staff psychologist not previously assigned to SCP-8142. Any memo generated by the phenomenon is to be collected, photographed, and stored in a fireproof safe in the Site-19 archives. Under no circumstances is Dr. Kessler to be allowed to read a memo more than once. **Description:** SCP-8142 refers to the recurring generation of handwritten notes appearing in the immediate environment of Dr. Mara Kessler, purportedly authored by her future self. The notes are always written in Dr. Kessler's handwriting, on standard Site-19 memo paper, with standard Site-19 memo paper watermark and serial number visible under UV light. The paper stock matches current inventory. The first incident occurred on 2025-11-03. **Addendum 8142-A: Personal Log of Dr. M. Kessler, Excerpt** I had been on Site-19 for eight months when it started. I was assigned to anomalous cognition, which felt ironic. The first note was on my desk at 07:42. I remember because I had just made coffee. It was folded once, in my handwriting. *Don't open Sector C on Thursday. It isn't a drill. -M* I laughed. I had no access to Sector C. It was a restricted biohazard wing I had only read about in briefings. I showed it to Dr. Armitage. He filed it. The second note appeared in my locker the next day. I had locked it. *They're listening through the vents. Burn this.* I didn't burn it. I put it in my pocket. By week three, the notes were daily. Sometimes twice a day. They always appeared where I wasn't. In my coat pocket after a shift, under my pillow, in the bathroom stall I used on the third floor. The paper was always the same. I kept the paper locked in a small steel box I bought off-site. The next morning, there was another memo on top of the box. The Foundation got involved. They checked the cameras. There were no blind spots where I was. They checked the paper. The serial numbers were legitimate, pulled from my office printer's stock. They checked me. MRI, EEG, psychiatric eval. Dr. Hargrove said I was under stress and exhibiting signs of sleep deprivation and dissociative ideation. He suggested I was writing them myself and forgetting. I wanted to believe him. I needed to. The notes got worse. *03:17. The red door. Don't trust Chen. He wasn't there in the first timeline.* Chen was my supervisor. He had been there for twelve years. I had never seen a red door on Site-19. Site-19 has no red doors. *You told me to run. I ran. The containment failed anyway. I'm sorry.* I started keeping a journal to prove I wasn't writing them. I wrote down what I ate, what I dreamed. The notes started referencing the journal. *You wrote about the tuna sandwich on Tuesday. You lied about the mustard.* I hadn't written about mustard. Then the contradictions started. A note said my brother was alive. My brother died in a car accident in 2011. I had a photograph of his funeral on my desk. The note said, *Call him. He misses you.* I called my mother to check. She cried and said she wished I would stop asking. The Foundation considered external influence. SCP-8142 was moved to a windowless isolation room for 72 hours with no paper stock. The room was swept for hidden compartments. Cameras recorded continuously. On the third night, a memo was on my pillow. *You keep the paper locked away. I keep it locked away. It doesn't matter.* I stopped sleeping. I started seeing the handwriting in condensation on windows. I was sure I was losing my mind. They brought in a consultant from Site-17 who specializes in memetic and psychic containment. He suggested testing for influence from SCP-███, a cognitohazardous entity housed two levels below my old office. The entity was known for inducing false memories and self-harm ideation in adjacent personnel. We moved me. The notes stopped for four days. On the fifth day, a note appeared in the new room, taped to the inside of my supply closet door. *They moved you. Good. Now listen. The breach isn't Sector C. It's you. Stop reading.* I told them I hadn't read it yet. They photographed it before I touched it. I read it anyway. The last note I received was on 2026-01-14. The handwriting was shaky, the ink smudged as if written with a wet hand. *I'm tired. The paper is bleeding through. I can hear you thinking about not trusting me. You shouldn't. None of this is real. The containment is already breached. It was breached in 2024. You just haven't remembered yet. -M* I haven't found a note since. I haven't slept through the night since. I don't know if I am being warned, or being warned away from something. I don't know if I am writing these to myself in a fugue state, or if something is writing them through me. The paper is always the same. The handwriting is always mine. I am scared to trust my own memory. I am scared not to. I am filing this log because Dr. Armitage said I needed to have an official record. If you are reading this, please check the safe. I put the last note in there. I told myself I wouldn't read it again. I read it again this morning.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates a strong understanding of the Foundation's clinical documentation style while effectively weaving in the psychological horror elements requested. The piece successfully adopts the SCP format with proper containment procedures and clinical language, then transitions into the researcher's personal perspective as specified. The narrative structure is well-executed, beginning with mundane notes and escalating to increasingly disturbing contradictions that blur the line between reality and delusion. The progression from simple warnings to reality-contradicting statements (like the dead brother being alive) creates genuine unease. The ambiguity between temporal anomaly and psychological manipulation is maintained throughout, fulfilling the prompt's core requirement. The characterization of Dr. Kessler is believable and sympathetic. Her rational attempts to explain the phenomenon, followed by growing desperation as conventional explanations fail, feels authentic to how a researcher might respond. The Foundation's methodical investigation approach also rings true to the SCP universe. However, the piece has some structural weaknesses. The transition between the clinical SCP format and the personal log feels somewhat abrupt, and the voice occasionally wavers between clinical detachment and personal terror. Some exposition feels forced, particularly when explaining Foundation procedures that would be obvious to the narrator. **Item #:** SCP-7143 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** All instances of SCP-7143-A are to be documented and sealed with standard reinforced steel plating from the interior side. Foundation personnel are forbidden from entering SCP-7143-B under any circumstances without Level 4 clearance and direct authorization from the Site Director. Monitoring of known SCP-7143-A instances is to be conducted remotely via thermal and motion sensors. Personnel assigned to monitoring are to rotate every 72 hours due to reported psychological distress. Any instance of SCP-7143-A found in a populated area is to be reported to Site-19 for immediate relocation of the host structure. All recovered documents from SCP-7143-B are to be catalogued under Project ARCHIVE. Personnel who handle archival material for more than four hours are to undergo mandatory psych evaluation. **Description:** SCP-7143-A refers to an unmarked, matte-black wooden door approximately 2.03 meters in height and 0.91 meters in width. Instances have been identified in 47 abandoned structures across 19 countries as of 2026-03-11. Structures include derelict factories, condemned apartments, decommissioned subway stations, and one former Soviet bunker. All instances are identical in construction, material composition, and wear pattern. Each door is set into a wall where no door previously existed, with no visible hinges, keyhole, or manufacturer markings. Around the doorknob area, a consistent pattern of fine, parallel scratches is present on all instances, measuring approximately 8-12 cm in length and appearing to be made by a fingernail or similar keratinous material. When opened, SCP-7143-A leads to SCP-7143-B, a non-Euclidean archival complex. The interior space is architecturally impossible. Corridors branch and loop without intersecting, ceilings exceed 30 meters in height while floor space remains constant, and recorded distances between waypoints do not correlate with travel time. The environment is perpetually lit by a diffuse, sourceless amber light. Temperature remains constant at 18.3°C. Air is breathable and contains trace amounts of ozone. SCP-7143-B consists of endless stacks of shelving units containing documents, data crystals, and bound ledgers. All materials are written in languages predating known human civilization, though 73% are translatable via Foundation linguistic databases. The content consistently references a prehistoric global civilization referred to in recovered texts as the "First Custodians." **Addendum 7143-01: Exploration Logs** *Log 7143-01-A. Mobile Task Force Zeta-9 "Bookworms" entry.* Team entered via Instance-19, former textile mill, Detroit. Door opened without resistance. Dr. Aris Thorne: "It's... quiet. Too quiet. The stacks go up forever." Upon first hour of exploration, team recovered Document 7143-B-04. Excerpt: > *...the Containment Breach of Year 0 was not a failure of will but of design. The Vaults were meant to hold the Quiet Things, but the Quiet Things learned to be loud. The cities fell not to fire but to forgetting. We burned the maps and buried the names. The Archive remains so that no one may repeat our error.* Later in the same wing, personnel discovered a personnel file cabinet labeled "THE ORDER OF THE SEALED EYE." Within were files for current Foundation staff. File 7143-P-881: Subject: Dr. Elena Mirov, Site-19 Researcher. DOB: 1991. File date: 12.04.1327. Marginalia in unknown script reads: "She will ask about the doors. Do not tell her." File 7143-P-902: Subject: Dr. K. Aris Thorne. File date: 11.09.1284. Status listed as "Deceased - Incident 7143-B-09." Thorne reported acute anxiety upon viewing. **Addendum 7143-02: Removal Entities** *Log 7143-02-B. MTF Zeta-9, Day 3.* At 02:14 local time, Section 7-G was observed undergoing active removal. Entities resembling humanoid figures in bulky, yellow hazmat suits with no visible faces were systematically removing entire shelving units. The units were lifted and phased through the walls. Dr. Thorne attempted approach. Entities ceased activity, turned in unison, and retreated into a side corridor at speeds inconsistent with bipedal locomotion. No vocalizations or equipment sounds were recorded. One entity dropped a containment tag. Tag reads: "REMOVE BEFORE NEXT CYCLE. DO NOT READ." No further activity was observed in Section 7-G upon return. The shelves were gone, leaving only rectangular discoloration on the floor. **Addendum 7143-03: Unauthorized Access** Review of SCP-7143-B security footage, recovered from embedded crystalline recorders, revealed multiple unauthorized entries. Footage from 2147-09-03 shows an individual matching the physical description of O5-3 entering via Instance-07, Prague. He spent 11 minutes in the archive and photographed a single document. Footage from 2199-11-21 shows an individual matching O5-7. He was accompanied by two unidentified personnel in Foundation attire. He placed a small metallic object on a shelf and left. O5 Council has denied all knowledge of SCP-7143-B. O5-3 and O5-7 have refused to comment on the recovered footage. **Addendum 7143-04: Recovered Document Excerpt** Document 7143-B-19, translated: > *To the next who find this door: We left it open on purpose. The scratches are a warning. Do not turn the knob. Do not look too long. The Archive is not a library. It is a quarantine notice. The Foundation you know is ours, renamed seven times. You are us, again. The Quiet Things are still quiet because we are still watching. If you see the yellow suits, run. They are not cleaning. They are editing.* The door instances continue to appear. As of this writing, 12 new SCP-7143-A instances have been reported in the last month alone.

+ Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The briefing said the colony of Kesh was divided. It said the High and the Low did not intermarry. It said the Low, who had grown broad in the chest and slow in the joints under the heavy gravity of the inner valley, resented the High, who were tall and narrow and lived in the cliff terraces where the air was thin. It said the High controlled the water and the Low controlled the stone. Envoy Lian had memorized the briefings on the flight from the orbital station. She was twenty-four, first posting, and she had been told to keep to the delegation, to speak only in the presence of an interpreter, to do nothing that might be read as familiarity. The reception was in the Hall of Accord, a vaulted room cut from basalt. The stone was old, older than the colony, quarried from the world itself. Carved into its ribs were glyphs no one in the delegation could read: a serpent eating its tail, a woman holding a pomegranate, a labyrinth with a single entrance. Old Earth myths, the guide had said, brought by the first ships and set in stone because paper rotted. After the speeches, when the ministers were drinking a bitter tea that stained the tongue, Lian slipped out the service door. Protocol said no. The air outside was warm and smelled of dust and cooking oil. The market was not in the briefings. It lay in the shadow of the Hall, between stone houses whose walls were patched with newer stone. The Low walked there with their children, and the High walked there too, descending the stone steps in small groups. They haggled over root vegetables and woven cloth. A woman with the High’s narrow face and the Low’s broad hands sold honey in clay jars. A man with the Low’s stocky build wore a High’s woven sash. Lian stopped at a stall where a boy carved small animals from soapstone. He showed her a hare, then a fish, then a creature with too many legs. “For the tourists,” he said in the trade tongue. His accent was neither High nor Low. She asked, “Do you sell them to both?” He laughed. “Who else would buy?” She walked further. The street was lined with lintels carved with the same old myths. Under a lintel of a tree with roots and branches both reaching for the sky, an old woman sat mending nets with a High woman who was perhaps her daughter-in-law. They spoke quietly, and the High woman’s hand rested on the old woman’s shoulder. No interpreter was needed. The market had its own grammar. She had been gone forty minutes. When she returned to her quarters, the door was already open. Commander Hara stood inside, his uniform too neat for the heat. “You were not in the reception hall,” he said. “I needed air.” “You needed to be where we could see you,” Hara said. “The High see you walking alone and they will say the Union does not respect them. The Low see you walking alone and they will say you are spying.” Lian felt the familiar heat rise in her face. “I saw them trading together.” “You saw a market,” Hara said. “Do not confuse a market with a polity.” He set a data-slate on the table. “Tomorrow you will request an audience with Minister Varro. She is Minister of Science.” “She is not a scientist.” “She is Minister of Science,” Hara said. “She is also the person who decides whether you stay or go.” Minister Selene Varro received her in a small office above the stone quarries. The walls were bare except for a single carving of a winged bull, an old myth from a place Lian could not name. Varro was older, her hair cut short, her skin the color of the stone. She did not stand when Lian entered. “Envoy,” she said. “You walked the market.” Lian’s stomach tightened. “I was curious.” “Curiosity is a luxury for people who do not have to live with the consequences.” Varro poured tea. “Your briefings tell you we are divided by lineage. Is that what you saw?” “I saw people buying honey.” “You saw people buying honey. You did not see the water ledger. The High control the cisterns. The Low control the quarry. When the cisterns run low, the Low do not give stone. When the quarry is closed, the High do not give water. That is the division.” “But they were together.” “They are together because they must be,” Varro said. “That does not mean they are one.” She set the cup down. “You are offworld. You think you can see the truth by walking a street. Tell me, Envoy, what do you think you know about us?” Lian thought of the glyphs, the serpent eating its tail. “I think you have been telling the same stories for a long time. And that you still tell them together.” Varro studied her. For a long moment there was only the hum of the ventilation. “You are young,” Varro said at last. “You have not yet learned that stories can be true and still be used.” She leaned forward. “The Union wants us to sign a water-sharing accord. The High want the accord to be public. The Low want it secret, because they do not want their neighbors to know how much they need. What will you advise your Command?” Lian felt the test settle around her like dust. She could give the answer Hara wanted: support the High, be visible. She could give the answer the briefings wanted: caution, division. She said, “I will advise them to ask what the market wants.” Varro smiled, a thin movement. “The market wants honey. The polity wants water. You will have to learn the difference before you can speak for us.” She dismissed Lian with a nod. In the corridor, the stone was cool under her palm. The glyphs ran along the wall, patient, repeating.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Le Guin's distinctive style, particularly her anthropological approach to worldbuilding and her spare, contemplative prose. The author successfully creates a complex colonial society where the supposed divisions between High and Low peoples are more nuanced than official briefings suggest, echoing Le Guin's frequent exploration of cultural misunderstanding and the gap between official narratives and lived reality. The characterization of Lian as a young, curious envoy who challenges protocol feels authentic and well-motivated. Her decision to explore the market alone is believable given her youth and genuine curiosity about the world she's been sent to understand. The progression from her unauthorized exploration to the confrontation with Commander Hara to the testing conversation with Minister Varro creates a satisfying narrative arc that builds tension effectively. The worldbuilding is particularly strong, with the physical adaptations of the High and Low peoples feeling organic rather than forced, and the economic interdependence around water and stone creating believable political tensions. The recurring motif of ancient Earth myths carved in stone adds depth and suggests themes about cultural continuity and shared heritage that transcend supposed divisions. The dialogue, especially in the climactic scene with Minister Varro, crackles with political intelligence. Varro emerges as a formidable character who tests Lian's understanding while revealing the complexity of the situation. The conversation feels like a genuine battle of wits rather than mere exposition. The prose maintains Le Guin's characteristic restraint and precision. Sentences like "The market had its own grammar" and "She felt the test settle around her like dust" demonstrate elegant economy of language. The imagery is vivid but never overwrought, from the basalt hall with its ancient carvings to the market's sensory details. However, the piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in explaining the political dynamics. Some transitions feel slightly abrupt, and while Lian's final answer about "asking what the market wants" is thematically appropriate, it feels somewhat predictable given the setup. The ending strikes the right tone of complexity without false resolution, staying true to Le Guin's preference for ambiguous conclusions that reflect real-world political complexity. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 9: Polymerase Chain Reaction** The solar panel rig on the roof of the water tower flickered every time a cloud passed over the ash-stained sun. It was a jury-rigged lattice of salvaged HelixCorp rooftop tiles wired through a car alternator and a prayer, and it made the lights in the lab stutter like a dying firefly. That was the problem with running a thermocycler off daylight. The voltage dipped, the heating block stuttered, and my PCR tubes risked a half-denatured run that would give me nothing but expensive sludge. I pressed my palm to the side of the old toaster oven I’d converted into a cycler. It was hot enough to burn through my patched glove. Inside, a row of microtubes rattled. Each held a slurry of maize DNA pulled from last year’s dead cobs and a fragment of HelixCorp’s Gold-7 rice, the one they’d sold to the Midwest cooperatives before the Collapse. Gold-7 was beautiful. It grew fast, sweet, and yellow as butter. It also carried the kill-switch. The corporations hadn’t been stupid. They’d been precise. Every engineered crop came with a methylated suicide cassette, a little epigenetic timer that methylated and degraded the transgene after one meiosis. You planted the seed, you got one good harvest, and then the next generation grew stunted, chlorotic, and sterile. The brochure had called it “Generational Stewardship.” The farmers called it rent. The settlement, New Sump, had been living on the rent for three years now. We were down to scavenging the last viable first-generation stock. I was trying to splice the Gold-7’s yield gene into a feral teosinte backbone that had survived the blight, hoping the wild genome would hold it long enough for two, maybe three harvests. It was illegal, it was stupid, and it was the only thing keeping the kids from chewing bark. The lab smelled of ozone and old agar. My bench was a door laid across cinderblocks. A centrifuge spun from a modified blender motor. A pipette was a repurposed insulin syringe with the plunger calibrated by hand. On the wall, a printout of a HelixCorp primer sequence was taped over a water stain. I’d memorized it years ago, before I learned what it was for. A knock rattled the tin door. “Contract’s here,” said Hana, my runner. She didn’t wait for permission. She set a dented thermos on the bench. Inside, sealed in a vial of saline, was a swab. Human. “Who?” I asked. “Name’s Voss. From the Ashen Road. Says you’re the only one who still runs a real PCR without a corporate license.” I didn’t like contracts. The last one had been for a fever suppressor splice for a foreman’s daughter. I’d used an untested retroviral vector, knocked out her cytokine storm, and left her with hair that grew back white and a metabolism that ran hot enough to keep her from ever catching a cold again. She could see in the dark now, too. The physical toll was real. My own hands trembled sometimes from the lung rot patch I’d given myself two winters ago. I’d spliced in a moth’s cytochrome P450 to break down the particulate. It worked. It also made my sweat smell like almonds and gave me nightmares in color. “Why me?” “He wants a test, not a treatment. Wants proof his daughter is his.” I stared at the swab. Paternity tests were easy. Too easy. But Voss was paying in batteries. Real, sealed lithium cells, not the leaky junk we usually got. “Fine,” I said. “But I’m not making anything for you.” Hana left. I pulled the vial under the flickering light. The solar rig hummed, dipped, surged. The thermocycler beeped, a cycle complete. I pulled the maize tubes out with tongs. The bands on the gel I’d run earlier were faint but there. The yield gene had copied. Maybe it would hold. I set up the PCR for the swab. Primers for the old HelixCorp lineage marker, the one they’d put in every citizen born after ‘38 to track patent compliance. It was a marker that degrades, too. One generation. If Voss’s daughter was his, the marker would be there, faint, half-erased. The machine whirred. The voltage dipped again and the heating block dropped five degrees. I cursed and adjusted the rheostat with a screwdriver, my left thumb brushing a scar where the patch had rejected once. The scar tissue was warm. Always warm. The gel ran. The bands showed up under the UV lamp I’d built from a blacklight and a cracked phone screen. Voss’s DNA. The daughter’s. A perfect match on the marker. I should have handed it over. Instead I stared at the second lane. A faint secondary band. Not HelixCorp. Wild type. A deletion. The kill-switch had already failed in her. The corporate DNA was breaking down faster than it should. That meant she was second generation. Born to a mother who’d been engineered. The marker should have been gone. It wasn’t. It was mutating. Voss wanted proof of blood. I had proof of something else: HelixCorp’s obsolescence was failing in some people. The timer was stuttering. The DNA was persisting, scrambling, rewriting itself. I could tell him no. I could tell him yes. I could sell him the batteries and keep the secret. I picked up the thermos and the vial of saline. The solar rig flickered overhead, throwing the lab into half-light. The maize tubes sat cooling on the bench, their future still one generation away from death. “Your daughter’s not yours by the book,” I said when Voss came in an hour later, breath steaming in the cold. “But she’s yours by the blood. The marker’s degrading wrong. It’s... persisting.” He stared at me. “What does that mean?” “It means HelixCorp’s rent might not hold forever,” I said. “And if you want me to keep quiet about it, you’ll give me those batteries and you’ll leave my rice alone.” He nodded once, fast. Outside, the sun caught the solar panels and the lights steadied for a moment. In the glow, the green shoots in my test trays looked almost alive.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk chapter successfully establishes a compelling post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering has created a dependency cycle through built-in obsolescence. The author demonstrates strong technical knowledge, weaving scientific terminology naturally into the narrative without overwhelming the reader. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, with vivid details of jury-rigged equipment like the solar panel rig made from "salvaged HelixCorp rooftop tiles wired through a car alternator and a prayer" and the converted toaster oven thermocycler. These details feel authentic and support the scavenged aesthetic of the setting. The protagonist is well-characterized through their actions and internal monologue, showing both technical expertise and moral complexity. The physical modifications they've undergone (almond-scented sweat, trembling hands, warm scar tissue) effectively illustrate the dangerous nature of their work while providing concrete consequences for their choices. The black market contract plot unfolds naturally, with the paternity test serving as both a source of income and a vehicle for revealing larger implications about the failing corporate genetic controls. The discovery that the obsolescence mechanisms are breaking down creates genuine tension and raises the stakes beyond the immediate transaction. The prose maintains a consistent, gritty tone throughout, with strong sensory details and technical authenticity. The dialogue, while limited, feels natural and serves the plot effectively. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither overly optimistic nor gratuitously dark - suggesting possibility while maintaining the harsh realities of the world. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the technical exposition could be more seamlessly integrated, and the character of Voss could have been developed slightly more to enhance the interpersonal dynamics of the contract negotiation. Model Output:
Arthur Neegan kept adjusting his collar, unused to the formal attire he had been instructed to wear. The stiff white shirt itched at his neck, and the dark jacket, cut for low gravity and boardrooms, hung awkwardly on a man who was used to canvas and thermal liners. The transfer vessel *Ares Relay* hummed around him with the patient, over-engineered diligence of all Martian colonial craft. Through the small porthole, Mars fell away. The ochre plains of his lease were a smear below, the immense vein he had found still unmarked on any official survey. He had been a mining engineer. He had been a first-generation settler who understood rock stress and water reclamation. He was not a man who was invited off-world by armed men bearing the insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. The insignia had been a stylized starburst over a closed fist. Diplomatic in name only, the colonists said. The men who had come to his prefab at dawn had been polite. They had offered coffee. They had also placed a rifle on his kitchen table while they waited for him to sign the transit waiver. “Mr. Neegan,” the escort officer had said, “you are to be conveyed to the station for consultation. It is routine.” Routine did not usually involve a sealed shuttle and a crew who did not speak to him. The *Relay* shuddered as it docked with Antares Station, a tumbling wheel of alloy and glass that served as the Corps’ forward post in the system. The airlock cycled with a sigh. Arthur was led down a corridor lined with polished steel and old-fashioned brass plaques, the retrofuturistic aesthetic the Corps favored — as if diplomacy were a matter of good manners and good lighting. He was shown into a meeting room. The table was long and real wood, an absurd luxury. At its far end sat a woman in a charcoal uniform with the same starburst insignia on her lapel. She was not young. Her hair was iron-gray, pulled back, and her eyes were the color of a winter sky on Mars. “Mr. Neegan,” she said, standing. “I am Director Lira Kallis, Antares Diplomatic Corps, Office of Resource Mediation. Please, sit.” He sat. The collar tightened. “Thank you for coming,” she said. “I know this is sudden. I assure you, it is not personal.” “Is it about the Azra?” he asked. She smiled, thinly. “Isn’t everything about the Azra now? You have found a vein of considerable size on Lease 7-Gamma. Our preliminary scans, conducted from orbit with your permission, suggest it is the largest unclaimed deposit in the Tharsis basin.” “I didn’t give permission,” he said. “You signed a lease with the Colonial Authority. The Authority signed a cooperation accord with Antares in 2179. It is all quite legal, Mr. Neegan. Very tidy.” He adjusted his collar again. “What do you want from me?” “Information,” she said. “And cooperation. The Azra you have found is not merely a fuel. It accelerates radioactive decay. That makes it invaluable for interstellar drives, yes. It also makes it a weapon of considerable unpleasantness. A gram properly placed can turn a city’s reactor into a brief, very bright sun.” Arthur felt cold. “I’m an engineer, not a—” “No one asks you to be a soldier,” Kallis said. “We ask you to be sensible. The corporations — Helion, Vesta Mining, the Earth Combine — would like to buy you out. The Colonial Authority would like to nationalize you. The Antares Corps would like to protect you.” “Protect me from what?” “From being made an example of.” She leaned forward. “There is a tug of war over Mars, Mr. Neegan. Earth wants the metal and does not want Mars to have leverage. Mars wants independence and sees Azra as its declaration. Antares sits between them, and we have a vested interest in neither side obtaining a monopoly on a material that can unmake worlds.” She slid a datapad across the table. On it was a contract. “We are prepared to offer you a personal security detail, a ten-year lease extension with full autonomy, and a research stipend to study the vein under our supervision. In return, you would agree to no extraction without our approval, and you would provide us with all geological data you collect.” “And if I refuse?” “Then you will be left to the corporations,” she said simply. “They will offer you more money than you have ever seen. They will also offer you lawyers, and then they will offer you a work camp when the price drops. The Authority will offer you a medal and then take the vein. You will be a footnote.” Arthur stared at the datapad. “Why me? I’m just one man.” “Because you are the only man who found it without a seismic array,” Kallis said. “That suggests the vein is shielded, or unusual, or both. We would like to know why. And we would like to know what else you might find.” Outside the window, the wheel of Antares Station turned slowly, showing the black of space and the pale curve of Mars. Somewhere out there, ships were moving, and fleets were being built, and men in offices on Earth were drawing lines on maps. “Are you going to tell me what Antares really wants?” he asked. She stood and walked to the window. “Antares wants stability. Stability requires that no one gets too much power too quickly. Azra is power. You are, quite accidentally, at the center of it.” He looked down at his collar, at the formal jacket that did not fit. “I just wanted to mine rock.” “I know,” she said. “That is why we are offering you a choice before someone else makes it for you. Sign, Mr. Neegan. Or do not. But understand that once you leave this room, you will no longer be a mining engineer. You will be a political asset. The question is whose.” The hum of the station filled the silence. Arthur Neegan, first-generation settler, adjusted his collar one more time and reached for the datapad.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a solid grasp of Asimovian science fiction conventions and successfully delivers on most of the prompt requirements. The author captures the retrofuturistic aesthetic through details like brass plaques, real wood tables, and the formal diplomatic setting, while establishing the political complexity that defines classic sci-fi. The world-building effectively balances intimate character moments with larger galactic implications, showing how Arthur's personal discovery has cascading effects across multiple power structures. The dialogue serves as the primary vehicle for exposition and character development, which aligns with Asimov's style. Director Kallis emerges as a compelling figure - calculating yet not entirely unsympathetic, representing institutional power while acknowledging Arthur's humanity. Her explanations of the political landscape feel natural rather than forced, and her final ultimatum carries genuine weight. Arthur's characterization as an ordinary man thrust into extraordinary circumstances works well, though his responses occasionally feel somewhat passive. His discomfort with formal attire and diplomatic settings effectively establishes his fish-out-of-water status, and his simple desire to "just mine rock" provides emotional grounding. The prose maintains appropriate restraint, avoiding overwrought descriptions while still providing vivid scene-setting. The pacing builds tension effectively through the journey from Mars to the station and into the negotiation. The ending appropriately leaves Arthur's decision ambiguous while making clear the stakes involved. However, some elements feel predictable - the "ordinary person discovers valuable resource and becomes political pawn" setup follows familiar patterns. The dialogue, while functional, occasionally lacks the sharp wit that distinguished Asimov's best work. Arthur's characterization, while believable, could benefit from more distinctive personality traits beyond his engineering background and discomfort with politics. The piece succeeds in establishing the larger intrigue and stakes as requested, with hints about corporate interests, colonial independence movements, and the weaponization potential of Azra. The world feels lived-in and politically complex without becoming overly complicated for a single chapter. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 88.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom smells like vinegar and hot metal, and under the safelight everything is the color of old blood. My prints hang on the line like ghosts, curling at the edges while the developer does its slow work. Elliot is at the enlarger, shoulders hunched in that thrift-shop-nu-goth coat he always wears, the one with the frayed velvet collar and too many pockets. He’s 19. I’m 25. I tell myself the difference is nothing, just six years and a whole different decade of being alive, and then I tell myself to shut up because I’m Dani and I’m not supposed to overthink. I’ve been watching him since September. Experimental Photography with Professor Marin. He sits in the back, quiet intellect, the kind of kid who takes notes in pencil and actually looks at people when they talk. Soft demeanor. Killer style. He never raises his hand, but his work is all sharp angles and bruised light. I’m the one who always raises my hand. I’m the one who takes charge in group projects, who tells people what lens to use, who kisses first. That’s my brand. Bold. Defined. Elliot isn’t defined. That’s what’s been messing with me. We got paired for the final because Marin likes “unexpected chemistry.” He put my name next to his on the board and I felt my jaw clench. Perfect. I could finally talk to him without it being a whole thing. Late nights in the darkroom were supposed to be about the project: body as archive, something about self-portraits and negative space. It’s been three weeks of this. Tonight he’s developing a self-portrait where he’s covered his face with his hands, just the outline of his jaw visible. The red light makes his skin look translucent. “You’re good at this,” he says suddenly, without looking at me. “The timing. You know when to pull it.” “Thanks,” I say, because I’m Dani and I don’t do false modesty. “You have a good eye for composition. You could be doing this alone.” He laughs, a small, surprised sound. “I don’t want to do it alone.” The enlarger hums. My phone buzzes silently in my pocket. Once. Twice. I know it’s my roommate asking if I’m coming home. I ignore it. I’m focused. Elliot dries his hands on a rag that’s been used a hundred times. The red light catches the silver in his hair, the little bit he’s dyed black at the roots. He’s wearing a choker and a band t-shirt under his coat. His fingers are long and careful. “I’ve been thinking,” he says. He says it like he’s testing the weight of the words. “About the project. About... me.” I want to take charge. My instinct is to lean in, ask the right question, make him feel safe. But I’ve been practicing not doing that. I’ve been practicing letting people speak. “Okay,” I say. I keep my hands in the tray, watching the print bloom. “I’m listening.” He stares at his own hands in the red dark. “I think I’ve been trying on masculinity like it’s a coat. Like yours.” He gestures vaguely at my own outfit — leather jacket, red lip, the whole assertive-art-student uniform I’ve curated since I was 18. “And sometimes it fits and sometimes it chafes. And I’m not sure I want to keep wearing it, or if I just want a different kind of coat.” The safelight makes everything honest. No flinching. My chest does something stupid. Excitement, first. Because I’ve never been around someone who’s actively interrogating themselves in real time. It’s thrilling, like watching someone develop a photo they’re not sure they want to see. And then protectiveness, immediate and inconvenient. He’s 19 and he’s telling me this in a room that smells like chemicals and feels like a confessional. I want to tell him it’s okay, that he’s allowed to take his time, that no one gets to rush him. And then, underneath that, confusion. I’ve always been attracted to defined things. Men who knew exactly what they were, who leaned into it. Broad shoulders, certainty, the kind of guys who could take what I gave them and give it back harder. Elliot is soft. He’s quiet. He’s questioning. He’s he/him for now, and he might not be later, and the thought makes my stomach turn in a way that isn’t disgust. It’s vertigo. “Does it bother you?” he asks, finally looking up. His eyes are dark in the red. “That I’m... not sure?” I could lie. I could tell him I love the mystery. I’m Dani, I’m good at smooth lines. “It’s new for me,” I say instead. Because the truth is a better developer. “I’m used to liking people who are... settled. And you’re not. And I think that’s why I can’t stop looking at you.” He blinks. The print in my hands is almost done. I lift it out, rinse it under the running water. The sound is loud in the small room. “I’m not trying to be confusing on purpose,” he says, voice thin. “I just... I like the idea of being gentle. I like dresses sometimes. I like the word boy, but I don’t like being... small. I don’t know.” I want to reach for him. My hand actually twitches toward his shoulder before I stop it. Take charge or give agency. That’s the war in my head every time I’m with him. If I touch him, am I comforting him or claiming him? If I ask more questions, am I guiding him or interrogating him? So I do the hardest thing I know how to do: I wait. “I’m not going anywhere,” I say quietly. “Whatever coat you end up in, you can wear it here.” He exhales like he’s been holding his breath since the semester started. “You’re not... weirded out?” “I’m turned on,” I admit, because the red light makes honesty cheap and I’m tired of performing. “Not in a creepy way. In a... I don’t know. I like watching you figure it out. I like that you’re soft and you’re sharp at the same time.” He smiles, a little crooked. “You’re very direct.” “I’m working on it.” My phone buzzes again in my pocket, insistent. I don’t check it. I’m focused on the way his jaw tightens when he’s nervous, on the way the safelight makes his thrifted coat look like armor he’s not sure he needs. We hang our prints to dry. His is next to mine. Mine is a stark black-and-white of my own hands gripping a camera too tight. His is the outline of a face, hands covering everything except the mouth. “Can I show you something?” he asks. I nod. He pulls out his phone — the screen is a soft blue in the red room — and shows me a sketch. A self-portrait with longer hair, a dress, the same quiet eyes. “I haven’t shown anyone,” he whispers. I look at it and feel that vertigo again, but this time it steadies. Because he’s letting me see it. Because he’s choosing to. “Thank you,” I say. He nods, and for a second we’re both just standing there in the darkroom, two people in uncharted territory, not touching, not taking charge, just existing in the same red light. My phone buzzes a third time. I’ll answer it later.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive art student while showing her vulnerability when confronted with unfamiliar territory. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically, with the red safelight creating an intimate, confessional atmosphere that enhances the emotional revelations. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and well-developed. Her attraction is portrayed with complexity - excitement at witnessing self-discovery, protectiveness, and confusion about her own identity preferences. Elliot emerges as more than just a catalyst for Dani's growth; his vulnerability and self-exploration feel genuine rather than performative. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. The sensory details of the darkroom - the vinegar smell, the red light, the chemical processes - ground the narrative in concrete reality while serving the metaphorical framework of development and revelation. The photography metaphors are woven naturally throughout without becoming heavy-handed. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, capturing the tentative quality of their conversations without becoming stilted. Dani's directness contrasts effectively with Elliot's more hesitant speech patterns, reinforcing their character differences. The pacing allows for proper emotional development without rushing toward resolution. The ending maintains appropriate uncertainty - both characters are in "uncharted territory" - which feels honest rather than artificially positive. The piece avoids the trap of solving complex identity questions too neatly. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly repetitive, and a few instances where the metaphorical language borders on being too neat. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece.
